items.title: Disgust, Desire, and Durian
items.description:
How Southeast Asia’s famously pungent fruit became a source of cultural identity and global demand.

The post Disgust, Desire, and Durian appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
In 2019, 550 students evacuated the University of Canberra’s library because of one fruit: durian. Its sulfuric odor had been mistaken for a gas leak, a common occurrence that has grounded planes and baffled fire departments worldwide. Known colloquially as the “King of the Fruits,” durian commands attention with its pungent scent and spiky husk. Despite these seemingly unsavory qualities, durian’s sweet flesh has created a multibillion-dollar consumer market that fuels economic growth in countries like Vietnam, Malaysia, Cambodia, and Thailand. Central to Southeast Asia’s ecological systems, economic development, and sociopolitical organization, durian’s overpowering presence shapes local customs and mobilizes transnational supply chains, testifying to the sensorial hold that plants have over us.

For those unacquainted with the peculiar odor, taste, and texture of durian, American botanist Francis Ramaley’s 1905 account offers a helpful starting point. He describes durian’s smell as a “rare combination of vile odors”: “first one thinks of rotten eggs, then of sewer gas and garlic and finally he gives up any attempt at a classification of the different smells.” By contrast, in one of the most vehement defenses of the fruit, British naturalist and “confirmed Durian eater” Alfred Russel Wallace waxes lyrical in his 1869 travelogue The Malay Archipelago:

A rich butter-like custard highly flavoured with almonds gives the best general idea of it, but intermingled with it come wafts of flavour that call to mind cream-cheese, onion-sauce, brown sherry, and other incongruities. Then there is a rich glutinous smoothness in the pulp which nothing else possesses, but which adds to its delicacy. It is neither acid, nor sweet, nor juicy; yet one feels the want of none of these qualities, for it is perfect as it is. […] In fact to eat Durians is a new sensation, worth a voyage to the East to experience.

These contrasting colonial accounts show that durian was just as polarizing then as it is today. More importantly, Ramaley and Wallace both recognized durian’s powerful effect on the senses and the intensely visceral responses it evoked, whether expressed in terms of disgust or desire. It is precisely this complexity and intensity that characterizes durian, a fruit whose importance in Southeast Asia goes beyond simple binaries like the detestable and the delightful, the economic and the cultural, or the local and the transnational.

Although the Durio genus has more than 28 recognized species, durian (Durio zibethinus) is the most commonly cultivated species for human consumption. At least 200 cultivars have been developed through human selection, and the plant has spread from its native Borneo, Sumatra, and Peninsular Malaysia to Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam. The characteristic smell of durian has been attributed to a combination of many different scent molecules, but scientists still struggle to pin down the exact compounds responsible, even with advanced chemical analysis techniques. The strong notes of fruity esters and sulphurous compounds are thought to serve as an important biological mechanism for attracting animals to consume the fruit and disperse its seeds.

There is a Balinese saying: “Buka durene hulung, masih ada ngaput,” which translates to “As with a fallen durian, there is someone who picks it up.”

Still, wild durians are relatively scarce because the fruit’s large seeds, tough husks, and thorny exterior mean that only large terrestrial mammals like elephants and macaques can participate in its seed dispersal. As a result, durian is now primarily found in human-managed landscapes, where it is grown semi-wild for household consumption or on commercial plantations. The method of commercial durian cultivation heavily depends on the region. For example, monoculture plantations are common in peninsular Southeast Asia, whereas on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, durians are grown in mixed agroforestry systems alongside other fruit crops and secondary forest.

Even before durian was recognized as a commercial crop, it was deeply significant to many Southeast Asian communities due to its cultural value. In Malaysia, the Indigenous Bersisi people celebrate the ripening of durian fruit with a feast. They create a communal space by setting up an ornamental railing with simple decorations and serdang leaves around the oldest durian tree, where cooked durians and other fruits are served wrapped in banana leaves. In Indonesian folklore, durian also often appears in proverbs and riddles. One example is the Balinese saying, “Buka durene hulung, masih ada ngaput,” which translates to “As with a fallen durian, there is someone who picks it up.” This proverb draws on the fact that durian fruits fall from the tree when they are ripe, suggesting that there will be somebody to help those going through a hard time. These practices highlight how durian is interwoven with the spiritual and cultural beliefs and practices of Indigenous communities in Southeast Asia.

The role of durian in Southeast Asian culture has also evolved alongside its cultivation as a cash crop, bringing together traditional values and modern economic practices. Among the Baduy people in the Kanekes region of Indonesia, fallen durians are considered public property, and neighbors often help each other sell unattended fruit. These collective farming and trading practices embody shared cultural values that have since been recognized as offering an alternative vision of governance that maintains public trust. For Indonesians who practice Islam, in which charging interest is prohibited, durian trees have served as a type of collateral for farmers who use the profits from durian harvests to pay back lenders until their loans are repaid. Thus, in addition to being traditionally valued in Southeast Asian communities, durian has taken on new significance as these communities respond to economic, religious, and cultural influences.

Early colonial records reveal the danger of viewing durian solely in economic terms. In an 1886 report on the economic plants of the Straits Settlements, Nathaniel Cantley, the British-appointed superintendent of the Singapore Botanical Gardens, noted that the supply of durian failed to meet local demand. Cantley attributed the lack of accessible land for cultivation to a racist characterization of Indigenous Malays as “indifferent to money-making further than sufficient for their daily requirements.” This perspective is not just a relic of British colonial rule but also offers a warning against understanding the importance of plants solely through the lens of economic productivity.

More to Explore

Cucumber: The Plant That Moves More than You Think

Andrés Muedano
March 25, 2026
Be it with its curling tendrils or because of its desirable properties, the cucumber is defined by motion: vertical, horizontal, geographical, and digital.

Against the backdrop of Southeast Asia’s colonial history, durian’s signature smell can also be understood as a means of nationalistic self-assertion. In the comic short story “Durians” by Filipino author Alejandro Roces, the first-person narrator is blamed and punished for the village’s disasters—typhoons, floods, and even volcanic eruptions—because he never goes to church. His mother eventually forces him to attend church when the Japanese invade the Philippines and station troops in their village. The narrator brings durians as a gift for the Spanish priest but is thrown out when the priest cannot stand the fruit’s odor. The story ends with the narrator feasting on durians alone. Roces plays on durian’s polarizing smell by contrasting the local narrator’s love of the fruit with the foreign Spaniard’s intolerance. In this way, Roces confronts the Spanish missionary efforts and the Japanese occupation by appropriating durian’s characteristic pungency as a symbol of Indigenous pride—an image so enduring that literary critic L.M. Grow described Roces’s brand of realist satire as “durian humor.”

More recently, as China has become the world’s largest market for durian, the fruit’s distinctive odor has also become intertwined with East Asian identity. The female narrator in Asian Canadian author Larissa Lai’s novel Salt Fish Girlsearches for a cure for the lingering smell of durian on her body. This striking olfactory motif draws on durian’s intimate yet disruptive scent, as well as the fruit’s fraught history with import regulations, to assert an alternative form of Asian agency in a Westernized and de-odorized world. While Lai’s novel and the broader circulation of durian as a commodity in China position the fruit as a potential pan-Asian symbol, this broader identity can obscure the regional specificity that makes durian a source of pride for Southeast Asian communities.

These complicated cultural dynamics are mirrored in tensions surrounding the expansion of durian production in Southeast Asia to meet Chinese consumer demand. In 2020, Malaysia aimed to increase its durian exports to China to 8,000 tonnes annually, driving the expansion of monoculture plantations onto the unrecognized ancestral lands of the Indigenous Orang Asli. The resulting forest clearing caused biodiversity loss and disrupted cultural practices, leaving the Orang Asli unable to gather native plants central to their forest-honoring ritual, sewang. Ironically, as production expands, the traditionally valued durian now threatens to displace the very Indigenous communities that have long celebrated it.

At the same time, durian remains a symbol of national pride in countries like Thailand and Malaysia, where the fruit is presented as a prized gift to visiting Chinese officials as part of “durian diplomacy,” helping bolster durian trade networks. Demand has grown so great that export systems are being shaped around the fruit, from QR code tracing systems for cross-border supply chain transparency to a proposed “Smart Durian Fast Track” to expedite transnational transport, inspection, and certification. Durian’s cultural resonance, then, emerges as much from its place in evolving political and economic networks as from its longstanding role in traditional societies.

Ask anyone who has ever tried durian: they either love it or hate it or, at the very least, vividly remember the experience. Just as its peculiar smell and taste continue to resist description, durian continues to challenge our understanding of its ever-evolving role in the history, politics, and economics of Southeast Asia and beyond. Appreciating durian in all its full-bodied complexity requires a plant-focused approach that goes beyond traditional methods of study. The Plant Humanities Initiative at Dumbarton Oaks brings this interdisciplinary approach to exploring the evolving and entangled relations between plants and societies.

items.title: Can We Recover a Worldview Lost to Colonialism?
items.description:
Among the Ao Naga of northeast India, humans may have been just one kind of person in a world filled with spiritual beings.

The post Can We Recover a Worldview Lost to Colonialism? appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
How did people see the world before older systems were displaced by colonialism? This is a question faced by communities all over the world. Anthropologist Tiatemsu Longkumer considers it in regard to one particular group of people, the Ao Naga of northeast India.

Today, Longkumer writes, nearly all Aos are Christian, and none practice the community’s pre-colonial spiritual traditions. And because the Ao Naga did not keep written records before the nineteenth century, written sources can’t tell us how they understood the world.

In contrast to a binary of good and evil, tsüngrem, mojing, and temenen were all understood as entities capable of positive or negative action toward humans.

The earliest written records of the society were created by colonial administrators and Christian missionaries. One such account is “The Ao Naga Tribe of Assam,” written by American sociologist and Baptist missionary W. C. Smith in 1925. Smith described the society as an example of “primitive man” and argued that their worship was driven by a fear of “unknown powers.” He distinguished good spirits known as tsüngrem from bad ones called mojing and temenen.

The following year, British administrator and anthropologist J. P. Mills published “The Ao Nagas,” in which he argued that the Ao religion was not a system of moral rules but instead a set of ceremonies calling on “deities” for help. He laid out a system of supernatural presences, defining “Lichaba” as the godlike chief of tsüngrem.

Since Smith and Mills’ time, Ao Naga Christian theologians have become the foremost experts on their community’s pre-Christian religion. Because these scholars work within a Christian framework, Longkumer writes, they are mainly interested in traditional beliefs and practices as precursors to the full divine revelation represented by the community’s conversion to Christianity.

More to Explore

The Changing Meaning of “Mysticism”

Livia Gershon
August 24, 2021
People who don't follow organized religion sometimes describe themselves as spiritual. But this idea isn't a recent invention.

In an effort to reconstruct what Ao Naga beliefs looked like before they were refracted through Christianity, Longkumer turns to animism, a broad term for worldviews in which humans are just one kind of “person,” with the capacity to be in relation to other entities, including the spirits of rivers and mountains.

Longkumer suggests that Mills’s distinction between morality and ceremony confused the reality of Ao practices, which emphasized the ethical practice of living in harmony with the spiritual world. He argues that Lichaba, an anthropomorphic spirit, should be viewed as just one among many tsüngrem, and that—in contrast to a binary of good and evil—tsüngrem, mojing, and temenen were all understood as entities capable of positive or negative action toward humans.

Similarly, Longkumer suggests that traditional Ao Nagas did not separate tanüla—a concept something like “spirit” or “soul”—from the material world. They believed that humans and other persons possess tanüla as part of their essence, but that humans are unique in having multiple tanüla, reflecting their diverse inner qualities and external relationships.

Longkumer acknowledges that it is impossible to really know how the Ao Naga saw the world two centuries ago, but he argues that animism can help evoke the complexity of a system that was different from, but no less rich than, the Christian one that followed it.

items.title: Beware of the Meeting Minutes
items.description:
What gets lost when spoken conversations become part of the historical record?

The post Beware of the Meeting Minutes appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Talk-talk, said Winston Churchill (reputedly), is always better than war-war. But how is such diplomatic talk-talk recorded for posterity? Until relatively recently, history has depended mostly on written records. Those are never the same as conversations, which by their very nature are ephemeral. The recollection, reconstruction, and/or condensing, in the “minutes” of a meeting, of what was said is the issue sociologist David R. Gibson explores.

Converting “talk with all its complexities, disfluencies, ambiguities, and occasional disarray, into a written record of who said what,” writes Gibson, is no easy task. Every historian should be aware of the potential pitfalls of this fraught form of translation. And not just historians. With so much of the news reliant on anonymous sources, the issues raised are important for a functioning democracy as well.

“We might say that minutes are not merely taken, but actively made, and the minute-takers are equally minute-makers, sometimes with input from others.”

Meeting minutes, writes Gibson, are “traces of words uttered behind closed doors, but they often have the appearance of a verbatim report, and even when they do not, it is tempting to read them that way, lulling us into erroneous conclusions about who said what, how they said it, and whom they were in agreement with.” Such minutes in the official compendium of “major U.S. foreign policy decisions and significant diplomatic activity” that is the State Department’s Foreign Relations of the United States (FRUS) series are given the imprimatur of history. But what exactly are they? (FRUS holdings begin with the Lincoln administration and are amply voluminous; there are, for instance, 25 volumes for the Kennedy administration and a planned 48 volumes for the Clinton administration.)

Minutes may be edited after the fact, by “the minute-taker or someone else,” notes Gibson. Members of the Soviet Union’s Politburo were neither the first nor the last who could and would alter minutes before they were disseminated. Gibson continues that “we might say that minutes are not merely taken, but actively made, and the minute-takers are equally minute-makers, sometimes with input from others.”

“Memories of talk” in after-the-fact minutes are as suspect as any other memories. “One problem with such recollections is that our ‘conversational memory’ is not especially good,” writes Gibson. “Experimental evidence suggests that we forget much of what was said in a matter of minutes. Another problem is spin.”

More to Explore

The President and the Press Corps

Jordan Friedman
November 6, 2025
Theodore Roosevelt was the first White House occupant to seek control over how newspapers covered him.

Spin, like gravity, seems to be a given. Gibson gives the example of Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, who “exaggerated his importance as an advocate for the temperate approach that brought the crisis to a peaceful resolution” during the heady days of the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962.

The reason we know this is that Kennedy’s brother, President John F. Kennedy, was secretly taping those National Security Council Executive Committee meetings in which the launch of World War III was seriously contemplated. So there is something to compare RFK’s retelling to.

The advent of relatively cheap audio recording in the second half of the last century began to allow for such comparisons of taped recordings with written records. They can be like night and day. British parliamentary proceedings, as one example, were taken by shorthand-reporters working five–ten-minute shifts. Recordings show these reporters corrected informal language and grammar, and omitted disfluencies (repetitions, non-lexical vocal sounds, all the “ums/ahs/likes” of actual conversation), making everyone sound a lot better, more, you might say, like, uh, statespersons. Another example, of a police interrogation transcript and audio recording of the same interrogation, showed how the transcript simply skipped over the police officers’ effort to cut a deal with the defendant by incorrectly noting that those passages were “unintelligible.”

Gibson’s own exploration compares the secret tape recordings of Kennedy and Nixon administration meetings with the minutes taken at those meetings by minute-takers unaware the meetings were recorded). In some cases, there are audio recordings, notes taken during meetings, and the finalized minutes produced afterward. It’s this process of transforming talk into an enduring record that concerns Gibson. What is preserved, what is deleted, what is added? Two examples: disagreements and ambiguities are glossed over in the name of consensus, and “conversational minutia” is sacrificed. For the study of history and its personalities, that’s a lot to sacrifice.

The problem of questionable minuting or transcription isn’t new. Of late-sixteenth-century official court transcripts, Gibson writes, “the notary’s task was to create an organizationally useful document, not a perfect record that would meet the sanguine expectations of historians centuries afterwards.”

items.title: What Does an Earthquake Sound Like?
items.description:
Seismologist Hugo Benioff spent decades turning seismic vibrations into signals he could study—and, eventually, hear.

The post What Does an Earthquake Sound Like? appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
In 1953, audio engineer Emory Cook released a unique album titled Out of this World. Upon playing it, listeners heard a reverberating boom and a narrator informing them: “This is a record of actual earthquakes.” Narration continued over a strange soundscape, explaining how tapes of earthquakes were sped up to make them audible. Those tapes came from the experiments of Victor Hugo Benioff, a seismologist who helped bring both seismological and musical instruments into the electronic age.

According to historian Matthias Dörries, these projects were deeply intertwined. Benioff had started in astronomy in 1917, working at both the Mount Wilson and Lick observatories. During downtime, Benioff practiced violin and tried to reconcile his love of music with his understanding of science.

In 1932, Benioff invented a new way of listening to the Earth: the strain seismometer.

Over the next couple of decades, Pasadena became “a major worldwide center for geophysical research,” Dörries explains. By 1926, Caltech was running the Seismo Lab with the Carnegie Institution, where seismologists like Beno Gutenberg and Charles Richter would deepen our understanding of earthquakes.

Benioff began work in seismology at Caltech in 1924. While Gutenberg and Richter focused primarily on theory, Benioff concentrated on instrumentation. At the time, seismometers primarily used weighted pendulums connected to pens or light beams that recorded vibrations on photosensitive paper. But these instruments had limited sensitivity.

Benioff began to experiment with electromechanical sensors, using a suspended weight connected to a transducer and a galvanometer. Then, in 1932, Benioff invented a new way of listening to the Earth: the strain seismometer.

More to Explore

Why Does Music in Science Fiction Sound Like That?

Angelica Frey
April 28, 2026
Imagining the sound of other worlds has a long past—and persistent creative limits.

Dörries describes the first instrument, installed “in the basement of the laboratory in the San Rafael Hills, with piers firmly fixed to the granite underneath the laboratory and cemented in with concrete.” The piers were 24 meters apart, with an iron pipe between them. Benioff left a tiny gap between one of the piers and the pipe. As vibrations and other changes in the Earth altered the size of the gap, Benioff recorded the changes with a transducer.

Greater sensitivity meant the instruments picked up other sources of vibration and strain: ocean surf, storms, traffic, and even sunrises. Benioff learned to “listen” to earthquakes, separating signal from noise.

“Benioff became an expert on how to materially transform the physical quantities of vibrational energy into electrical energy,” Dörries writes, “and then to record them over time in seismograms, which he read like musical scores.” He would soon use similar principles to experiment with electric instruments.

He experimented with transducers to create electric violins and cellos and filed patents in 1938. A concert at Caltech that June featured an “electro-cello” and a violin that the Los Angeles Times referred to as a “seismographic fiddle.” Benioff would later work on electric grand pianos, establishing a partnership with pianist Rosalyn Tureck.

Benioff used these “technologies of enchantment,” Dörries writes, “to bring unity and wholeness to technological and human culture.” He spent decades “listening” to earthquakes, including the largest ever recorded, in Chile in 1960. Dörries quotes seismologist Stewart Smith: “Benioff could finally hear the ‘music of the earth.’”

items.title: Teaching Students to Follow an Idea
items.description:
A five-step classroom exercise reframes research as an evolving scholarly conversation rather than a search for sources.

The post Teaching Students to Follow an Idea appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
I teach first-year academic writing courses in the University of Georgia English Department. Lately, I have been using JSTOR to help my students see research differently through an activity I call “Biography of an Idea.” Students begin with one scholarly article in JSTOR, usually from their discipline, and choose an idea, question, concept, argument, or even a citation that interests them. They then follow that idea backward and forward through scholarship: tracing where it came from, how other scholars have changed or challenged it, and what happens to it as it moves from one source to another. The goal is not simply to find more sources, but to experience research as an act of following knowledge. In this way, their paper becomes an intellectual conversation.

I developed this activity because students often perceive research writing as a series of requirements: finding scholarly sources, writing an annotated bibliography, citing sources, and producing a literature review. These requirements are useful, but they can also make scholarship seem like a collection of finished objects. Articles appear in databases, then students download them, extract information, and cite them. I wanted students to see something different: scholarship as a conversation that changes over time.

By following an idea backward and forward, students begin to see research not simply as finding information, but as encountering knowledge.

For “Biography of an Idea,” I ask students to select a scholarly article that connects to a question they are already exploring. The article does not have to provide the answer to their research question. In fact, it is often more productive if it gives them something to wonder about. I then ask them to choose one idea from the article. It might be:

  • A concept the author uses
  • A question the author raises
  • An argument that surprises the student
  • A disagreement between scholars
  • A term the student does not fully understand
  • A claim that makes the student want to know, “Where did this come from?”

That last question is where the research begins.

The research paper as a conversation

In academic writing, we often tell students that they need to “join the conversation.” I use that particular metaphor frequently, but I realized that students did not always understand what a scholarly conversation actually looks like. This is especially true for students from educational contexts where academic writing was not part of their training. Many of them come to my class and learn about it for the first time. The activity is especially useful for students who are new to academic writing.

“Biography of an Idea” gives them a way to see that conversation in action. Every conversation has a history: Someone says something. Someone else responds. Another person disagrees. Someone takes an earlier idea and applies it somewhere new. Another scholar changes the terminology. Sometimes an idea becomes so familiar that scholars stop citing the person who first introduced it. Sometimes an argument disappears for decades and then returns in a new form.

JSTOR is particularly useful for making this history visible because students can move among scholarly works rather than encountering each article as an isolated document. By following an idea backward and forward, they begin to see research not simply as finding information, but as encountering knowledge: deciding what questions are worth asking, learning the language that makes those questions searchable, figuring out which sources to trust, and making choices about whose ideas become part of their own work.

Assignment at a glance

Course: First-year academic writing.
Student level: First-year undergraduate.
Format: Individual assignment with in-class research and discussion.
Time: Approximately one week (two sessions).
Sources: One starting article and approximately three to five additional scholarly sources traced backward and forward.
Final product: A 250–1500-word “Biography of an Idea” that traces the development of the selected idea and explains how its meaning or use changes across sources.
JSTOR preparation: Students receive a brief introduction to JSTOR’s search, citation, and citation-tracing features before beginning the assignment.
Evaluation: The assignment is evaluated based on the quality of the student’s chosen idea, the relevance and range of sources traced, the accuracy of the research trail, and the student’s ability to explain how the idea develops across the scholarly conversation. For more, see Step 5.

Step 1: Find an idea worth following

Students start with a JSTOR article related to their research interests. For example, say, “Responsibility or Liability? Student Loan Debt and Time Use in College” (Quadlin and Rudel, 2015).

I tell them not to worry about finding the perfect article. At this stage, curiosity matters more than completeness. They read with a slightly different question than they might normally ask of a scholarly source: What in this article makes me want to know more?

In Quadlin and Rudel’s article, a student might become interested in the idea of student debt as either a responsibility that motivates them or a liability that constrains them. The student then writes briefly about why this idea caught their attention. This changes the starting question from What source do I need to fulfill the assignment? to What do I want to understand? Research begins with intellectual curiosity.

Step 2: Follow the idea backward

Once students have identified an idea, they review the article’s citations and references. I ask them to find at least one earlier source that appears to have influenced the idea and use JSTOR to locate and read it to understand the relationship.

For the Quadlin and Rudel example, one can trace the debate over whether educational debt encourages responsible behavior or creates financial constraints.

In this example, students look for two answers:

What did the earlier scholar say? and What did Quadlin and Rudel do with it?

Sometimes the relationship between the ideas above is straightforward, and sometimes it isn’t. Sometimes the chosen scholar revises or complicates the earlier argument. In any case, students begin to see that the citations are more than evidence that a writer did research. They are the evidence of a relationship between ideas.

Step 3: Follow the research forward

After moving backward, students move forward in their research.

Students then use the chosen article’s citation information to locate later scholarship that also engages with the article or idea.

Returning to Quadlin and Rudel, for example, later researchers have taken up the relationship between educational debt, time use, and students’ broader college experience. A student might ask if someone:

  • Adopted it?
  • Challenged it?
  • Renamed it?
  • Stopped using it?
  • Applied it to another community, historical period, discipline, or problem?
  • Discovered a problem with the original argument? 

Students begin to see an intellectual genealogy because they can see their idea has predecessors, descendants, disagreements, and adaptations.

Step 4: Notice what changes

In this stage, I ask students to put the sources next to one another and look for movement rather than summarizing each article.

In the Quadlin and Rudel example, the student might trace the idea this way:

  • Earlier scholars debated debt as responsibility or liability.
  • Quadlin and Rudel examined those possibilities through students’ patterns of time use.
  • Scholars after Quadlin and Rudel extended the conversation by connecting educational debt and time use to other dimensions of students’ experiences.

At this stage of their activity, students begin to realize that scholarly knowledge is not static. It changes as scholars revise questions, terms, arguments, and research context. This is also the moment where I begin to talk about the ethics of research. Some themes of questions I have brought to class include:

  • Who gets cited?
  • Who gets remembered in the field?
  • Whose terminology becomes standard?
  • What happens to an argument when later scholars adopt only part of it?
  • What knowledge becomes difficult to find because the language used to search for it has changed?

Step 5: Write the biography

The final product of this activity is a short “Biography of an Idea.” Students introduce the idea they selected, explain where they encountered it, and narrate what happened to it as they followed it through scholarship.

For the Quadlin and Rudel, a student might write:

My initial exposure to the idea that student loan debt influences students’ college experiences was through Natasha Yurk Quadlin and Daniel Rudel’s “Responsibility or Liability?” At first, I saw debt mainly as a financial issue. Reviewing their citations helped me see that scholars had already debated whether debt fosters responsibility or creates constraints. Tracing the conversation forward revealed how later researchers expanded these ideas to other areas of students’ lives. I started with a simple question about debt and ended up with a broader understanding of how financial circumstances shape the college experience.

From there, they bring in their sources to explain how and what they trace about the idea.

My rubric for assessing the quality of the assignment asks students to demonstrate six things:

  1. A clearly defined idea or question: The student identifies a specific idea, concept, argument, or question and explains why it is worth following.
  2. Accurate relationships among sources: The student correctly explains how earlier, central, and later sources relate to one another.
  3. Synthesis rather than summary: The student connects sources to show how the idea develops rather than discussing each source separately.
  4. Attention to change: The student identifies meaningful changes, disagreements, adaptations, or gaps in the scholarship.
  5. Reflection on learning: The student explains what following the idea taught them and how it changed their understanding of their field.
  6. Clear and accurate citation: The student appropriately cites the scholarly works they examined and provides enough information for readers to follow the research trail.

The result is still research writing, but students learn to summarize and synthesize sources, trace citations, evaluate evidence, and analyze arguments while also thinking about the production of knowledge itself.

The wildcard

Another reason I bring this activity into my writing classes is that my students are required to assemble a portfolio that includes a wildcard piece. This gives students an opportunity to include writing that does not necessarily fit the more conventional genres they have produced during the semester.

“Biography of an Idea” has become a piece students often submit for the wildcard. Others have created a multimodal version of it using text, images, quotations, citations, audio, video, or other media to show how the idea is inherited, transformed, contested, and reimagined.

More to Explore

Lies, Damn Lies, and…Primary Sources?

Nicole Donawho
July 15, 2025
An instructor shares her approach for teaching students how to evaluate historical materials and claims of veracity made by their originators.

I let them take both approaches because the portfolio also asks writers to reflect not only on what they researched, but on what happened to them as researchers. “Biography of an Idea” allows them to reflect on how following an idea through scholarship changed their understanding of research, their relationship to sources, and sometimes even the question they thought they were trying to answer. In a way, the wildcard visualizes what is difficult to teach directly: research changes the researcher.

What students learn about research

The activity teaches conventional research skills. Those might include searching JSTOR, following citations, identifying relevant scholarship, comparing sources, and synthesizing arguments. However, “Biography of an Idea” also helps students reconsider what those skills mean. They begin to see that a source is not simply “good” because it is scholarly, that a citation is not merely a requirement at the end of a sentence, and that a literature review is more than a list of what other people have said.

A common denominator in all these reactions is that my students begin to see research as a practice of knowledge-making. The above distinction is important to me as a writing instructor. Academic writing courses can easily become courses in academic conventions: where to put the citation, how many sources to use, how to format the bibliography, how to structure the introduction. I am not saying students do not need those conventions. However, those conventions become much more meaningful when students understand the intellectual practices underneath them.

Students begin to search JSTOR to recognize the choices involved in the research before they ever open an article. When students search JSTOR, they decide which terms to use, which results are relevant, which citations to follow, and which arguments deserve attention. Those choices shape the knowledge they ultimately produce as writers. By following an idea through scholarship, students can see how terminology shifts, arguments develop, and disagreements emerge, and how their own writing enters that process.

A small assignment with a larger purpose

I don’t expect every student to leave my academic writing course thinking like a historian, literary scholar, or researcher. They may never write another literature review after they graduate. But I do want them to leave knowing something about how knowledge works.

“Biography of an Idea” is deliberately small. A student can complete it with a handful of sources, and the activity can be adapted to different disciplines, levels of experience, and formats. What matters is not the size of the assignment but the shift in perspective it brings into the conversation. Instead of asking only, What does this source tell me?, my students begin asking: Where did this idea come from?, What happened to it?, Who changed it?, or Whose version survived?, leading them to think, What am I doing to it now?

That last question is perhaps the most important one as a writing instructor, because when students write research papers, they are not simply collecting knowledge that already exists. They are selecting, interpreting, connecting, and presenting knowledge for a new audience. “Biography of an Idea” gives them a way to see that process happening on a small scale before they attempt it in a larger research project. In doing so, it helps them understand not only how to produce academic writing, but how academic knowledge gets produced in the first place.

items.title: Building a Library in Wartime Paris
items.description:
Photos from the American Library in Paris reveal how librarians brought books to US troops during World War I.

The post Building a Library in Wartime Paris appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
The Germans began firing on Paris again on the fifth of August 1918. Mary Josephine Booth was familiar with the sound of the air raid sirens by then. If they came at night, she would jump out of her bed at the Hotel Petrograd, dress, take what valuables she had, and if the shelling was especially fierce, retreat to the basement. But if the sirens came during the day, then Booth, clad in her olive-green uniform, would remain at her post in an ornate building across the street from the Palais de L’Élysée. “We had to keep working to get the library ready to open,” she would later write.

Booth was one of hundreds of librarians who went to war alongside American troops during the First World War. In the summer of 1918, the 42-year-old woman from Illinois served with fellow recruits to the American Library Association’s Library War Service as they prepared to open an American library in the war-scarred French capital, pictures of which are now available from the American Library in Paris via JSTOR. Booth helped with unpacking and sorting the countless books that arrived from the home front, cataloguing titles for the new library (a project made more challenging by the lack of a Dewey Decimal reference guide) and selecting which would be sent to “our boys in the front trenches.”

When the United States entered the conflict, the American Library Association had not been well known. In fact, among other organizations doing war relief work, the ALA was, on occasion, mistaken for the American Laundry Association and the Australian Light Artillery. By 1920, the group would raise $5 million from the American public, build 36 camp library buildings, and distribute more than 10 million books and magazines to soldiers stationed at 5,000 locations across the United States and Europe.

Booth seemed like a natural fit for the Library War Service. She was a graduate of the Illinois State Library School, had worked as a librarian at Eastern Illinois Normal School for more than a dozen years, and she was eager to join the war effort in Europe. But the American Library Association did not initially warmly welcome women to the ranks of its war service. The organization saw the undertaking as an opportunity to masculinize the women-dominated profession, historian of librarianship Suzanne M. Stauffer says. Only men “of real executive ability” were officially permitted to be camp librarians, as the presence of women “would interfere with the freedom of the men in their camp life” and would deter “red-blooded he-readers” from using the libraries.

That was not Booth’s experience. She arrived in France in November 1917 as a Red Cross volunteer. Her first assignment was in a canteen at an aviation training center near Tours. There, she made ham, cheese, and jam sandwiches and built a makeshift library of her own. On January 21, 1918, she noted in her diary that there were “about 175 books ready to circulate,” purchased by a fellow canteener who had been given some money to “buy whatever was most needed.” Booth would later recall the popularity of the women’s library: “There were calls for mechanical books, as well as novels with lots of life and love, blood and thunder, and in contrast the poems of Milton and Browning.”

By 1918, the ALA had realized that it could not succeed in its mission without women librarians, though they were oftenrelegated to behind-the-scenes roles. In Europe, the director of the Army Library Service was Burton Stevenson, whose library at Camp Sherman in Ohio served as the basis for the Library War Service. Stevenson sometimes wondered how he, a Princeton dropout who became a librarian after marrying one, had achieved the position. He wrote to a friend from Paris, “my library work previous to about a year ago, was a sort of avocation, a sort of recreation which kept me in touch with books; so it seems strange to me sometimes that I should be the man selected to come to France to represent the A.L.A.” A photo in Stevenson’s office dated 1919 shows the American library staff. Booth, in her ALA uniform complete with tie, is gathered with five other women, including librarian-in-charge Elizabeth Gray Potter, and one other man.

The American library opened its doors at 10, Rue L’Élysée on August 29, 1918, as planned. The marble-columned entrance hall of the former home of the papal legate was taken up with a circulation desk; two large reception rooms with frescoed ceilings and mirrored walls had been converted into reading rooms; and the central hallway was lined with bookshelves for more than 7,000 titles. It was soon filled with men in khaki. “It was astonishing how quickly the soldiers discovered there was an American Library in Paris,” Potter noted.

Booth was quickly sent off on new missions. First, she organized the library of the new US military intelligence section (“several thousand books, English, French, Italian, German, especially strong in history, economics and military affairs”) and then, after the November 1918 armistice, she traveled through France sending books from the front back to Paris. “After the signing of the Armistice,” she later wrote, “the need of books was greater than ever; thousands of Americans in a strange land, all wanting to get home with nothing to do.”

Before returning to the library at Eastern Illinois Normal School (now Eastern Illinois University) in the summer of 1919, Booth’s last act was handing out magazines from the ALA to departing soldiers. She would go on to serve as a librarian at Eastern Illinois for another twenty-five years—and the American Library in Paris she helped to establish still exists today.

items.title: Why Italian Fascists Loved Samurai
items.description:
Japan offered Italian Fascists a powerful example of how ancient traditions could serve modern nationalism.

The post Why Italian Fascists Loved Samurai appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
The right-wing movements that emerged around the world in the mid-twentieth century were both highly nationalistic and willing to work across borders. And, as Michele Monserrati, a scholar of modern Italian studies, writes, that helps explain why Italian Fascists were obsessed with samurai.

Monserrati writes that Italians, and Europeans in general, got many of their ideas about samurai from a 1900 book by Japanese diplomat Nitobe Inazō, a strong supporter of Japan’s colonization of Korea. Titled Bushido: The Soul of Japan, the book was written in English to convey a vision of Japanese culture to a Western audience. It presented the samurai as similar to the chivalric knights of European legend, propelled to victory by honor, courage, and loyalty.

Samurai imagery gained prominence during World War I, which many right-wing Italians viewed as an opportunity to reinvigorate a militaristic form of nationalism.

This image influenced the Italian view of the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905, in which European journalists presented the Japanese soldiers as samurai-like paragons of discipline and self-sacrifice.

Monserrati writes that this was inspiring stuff for many young Italians, who—much like many in Japan—were frustrated with their country’s minor position in geopolitics and interested in modernization and building an imperial power. Samurai imagery gained prominence during World War I, which many right-wing Italians viewed as an opportunity to reinvigorate a militaristic form of nationalism.

One of these thinkers was Bartolomeo Balbi, who translated Bushido and other Japanese books. In particular, he was interested in the idea of honorable death, including ritual suicide. He likened seppuku to the mythological story of the Roman soldier Marcus Curtius, who rode his horse into a chasm to save Rome from destruction.

More to Explore

How Race Shaped New York’s View of Chinese Opera

H.M.A. Leow
May 29, 2026
In 1930s New York, Chinese opera was praised uptown but mocked in Chinatown.

Shimoi Harukichi, a Japanese writer from a samurai lineage, moved to Italy in 1915 and worked to align the nationalism of the two countries. He identified Fascism as a spiritual movement comparable to the bushido warrior ethos.

In one wild anecdote, Monserrati writes that Shimoi helped engineer an invitation from the Japanese soft drink company Calpis to have Mussolini offer an “inspirational message” to Japanese youth. Il Duce delivered a speech highlighting the commonalities between bushido and Fascism.

With actual samurai sidelined as Japan modernized in the nineteenth century, Italians were able to cherry-pick the aspects of the samurai’s image that they found most relevant. Some Fascists admired Japan’s use of Shinto shrines and ritual to endow its militaristic nationalism with spiritual power.

Others were particularly interested in Zen Buddhism, which Japanese thinkers including D.T. Suzuki argued was a key to bushido. Here the focus was not nationalism but a spiritual discipline that supposedly allowed warriors to accept death with equanimity.

Julius Evola, a Fascist intellectual who wanted Italy to abandon Catholicism for ancient Roman paganism, proposed that Zen was an outgrowth of an ancient “Indo-Aryan” religion mirrored by ascetic European traditions. Following World War II, he helped lionize kamikaze pilots who supposedly accepted death with a Zen-inspired inner peace. He became a major figure in the postwar Italian right and continued to use samurai as symbols of courageous resistance to materialism and modernity.

items.title: Ancient Rome’s Complicated Border
items.description:
What did Hadrian’s Wall actually do? Its history challenges the idea that walls simply separate one side from another.

The post Ancient Rome’s Complicated Border appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
We live in an age of hardened borders and militarized frontiers. Particularly since the September 11, 2001 attacks and then the Covid-19 pandemic, the supposedly borderless world of globalization has seen significant retrenchment and “re-bordering,” including the rise of nationalist movements hostile to immigration.

It doesn’t require a stretch to understand why what scholar Andrew Gardner calls the “lived complexities” of the Mexico–US border has helped give rise to the interdisciplinary field of Border Studies. And it’s easy to see why Hadrian’s Wall, the imperial Roman boundary across northern England, has been taken up by the relatively new discipline. For even though Hadrian’s Wall is more than 1,900 years old, it presents a classic case for the study of the ideas and the practices of a frontier between us and them, a formulation that works on both sides of a divide.

The wall marks neither the English–Scottish border nor the furthest northern extent of Roman Britannia.

Hadrian’s Wall is the place of continuing archeological discovery, even after all these years and explorations. As a UNESCO World Heritage Site, it’s also a famed tourist attraction, with thousands walking the entire 84-mile route of the wall’s National Trail every year, while hundreds of thousands visit sections of it. (See the Sycamore Gap.)

The wall also has, argues Gardner, “an even wider influence in popular culture, concomitant with its iconic status as a robust linear barrier.” He refers to its implicit use in Brexit and Scottish independence debates and, more benignly, its influence on the ice wall in George R.R. Martin’s epic A Song of Ice and Fire, a.k.a. Game of Thrones. Noting such absurdities as a movie Robin Hood walking the hundreds of miles between the White Cliffs of Dover and Hadrian’s Wall in an afternoon jaunt (Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves, 1991), Gardner also caveats that the wall’s “influence is frequently rooted in misconceptions.”

Construction of the stone wall began in 122 CE. It was named after the Emperor Hadrian, who toured the northern provinces of Germany and Britain in 121–122 to consolidate the empire’s frontiers. Hadrian himself likely inspected the wall’s ongoing work.

More to Explore

Ancient Rome: A City of Immigrants

Matthew Wills
August 17, 2026
A neighborhood beyond the Tiber became home to generations of Jewish and Syrian migrants who reshaped the imperial capital.

It should be noted that the wall marks neither the English–Scottish border nor the furthest northern extent of Roman Britannia. One hundred miles further north, the Romans built the 39-mile-long Antonine Wall, begun in 142 CE. This structure, at the narrowest part of Britain, was named after Emperor Antonius Pius, Hadrian having died in 138. As an earthwork with a wooden palisade, however, much less of Antonius’s wall has survived the ensuing millennia. The Antonine Wall was abandoned after about twenty years, while Hadrian’s Wall remained the frontier for nearly 300 years, until the demise of Roman Britain in the early fifth century.

Much of the stone used to construct Hadrian’s Wall and its forts and milecastles was recycled over the centuries, but the stone footings largely remain, as do the flanking ditches. The turf construction of the westernmost thirty miles of wall is its least studied section.

“As we know well from the large-scale changes of plan during the construction period, through to the later blocking of some gates at milecastles and forts, the Wall did not have a singular purpose or meaning, perhaps even not for Hadrian himself,” writes Gardner.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

It does not look forbidding today, but in its time the wall was a “robust boundary—within a broad militarized zone.” It caused significant settlement pattern changes both on the Northumbrian plain and further north into Scotland. “The complex interplay of accommodation and exclusion that is characteristic of borderlands,” was at play in the north of England (and the south of Scotland), just as it is in modern borderlands.

“The mixture of inequality, violence and interaction on the frontier creates local dynamics with far-reaching consequences,” writes Gardner of today’s world, but he is also speaking by analogy of ancient Rome and its far-flung frontiers. Rome defined the frontier, and the frontier defined Rome. The “continual duality of borders” is “not only dividing and fixing, but always also connecting and changing.”

items.title: The Women Who Sold Books Door to Door
items.description:
Three nineteenth-century memoirs reveal the risks and rewards of life on the road as a traveling bookseller.

The post The Women Who Sold Books Door to Door appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
In the second half of the nineteenth century, before the rise of public libraries, many people in remote parts of the United States got their hands on new books thanks to traveling salespeople. As literature scholar and archivist Jolie Braun writes, drawing on three memoirs from this era, women in that line of work had some distinct advantages but also faced serious hardships, both physical and social.

The booksellers visited homes and businesses with sample books, took orders, and then later delivered the books and collected payment. Braun writes that popular volumes included Bibles, farming and health manuals, biographies, and fiction. Ulysses S. Grant’s memoirs and the works of Mark Twain were popular choices. Many books published using this “subscription” model sold hundreds of thousands of copies.

Dumond described pride in her work’s “dissemination of light and knowledge among the masses.”

While the vast majority of book peddlers were men, some publishers recruited women with the idea that they would be well suited to sell books on health and hygiene to female readers, and also that customers would find them sympathetic.

In an 1868 account of her work selling books across northern Illinois and Indiana, Annie Nelles Dumond described taking up the work out of necessity. She wrote that, seeking to escape a difficult childhood, she married young to a man who turned out to already have a wife and children. A second husband abandoned her. So Dumond sought ways to support herself.

When she began selling books, she wore a mourning bonnet. She acknowledged that this was deceptive but wrote that it was “almost necessary to my self-preservation that my past should not be known.”

More to Explore

The Patron Saint of Bookstores

Jamison Pfeifer
October 5, 2019
100 years ago, Sylvia Beach, the first publisher of James Joyce’s Ulysses, opened the doors to her legendary bookstore, Shakespeare & Co.

Dumond described pride in her work’s “dissemination of light and knowledge among the masses.” By contrast, in an 1874 book on her own work as a bookseller, J. W. Likins of central California wrote that, despite knowing it was “honorable and legitimate” employment, “it seemed to me very much like begging.”

Likins, who took the job to support her family after her husband became too ill to work, wrote that some potential customers seemed curious or pitying. But a few men were angry to see a woman out on her own, demanding that she go home to take care of her family or incorrectly assuming that she was a suffragist.

More disturbingly, in a third autobiographical account Braun considers, published in 1881, a northern California peddler named Harriet Wasson Styer described a man telling her that, if she were his sister, he would murder her rather than allow her to canvass.

But much of Styer’s account suggested a fascinating experience. She recounted traveling to lumber camps and mining towns, admiring the wild landscapes, and coping with bed bugs and dirty stagecoaches.

Braun notes that all three peddlers were well aware that they were doing something many people believed was improper for a lady, but they took on the work out of a combination of necessity and a chance for adventure.

items.title: Minimalist Fiction in Six Short Stories
items.description:
The art of saying more with less, by Raymond Carver, Amy Hempel, Frederick Barthelme, Jayne Anne Phillips, Mary Robison, and Ann Beattie.

The post Minimalist Fiction in Six Short Stories appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Just like “love” in Raymond Carver’s iconic short story “What We Talk About When We Talk About Love,” “minimalism” is a contested term. Carver, the most famous minimalist, was averse to the label. While the origins of minimalism can be traced to modernist influences like Hemingway and Beckett, the style rose to prominence in the late 1970s and 1980s, with influential editor and teacher Gordon Lish helping shape and champion the work of several writers associated with it. But what do we mean when we talk about minimalism? Minimalist fiction is characterized by direct, highly compressed, densely allusive language. Much is left unstated, requiring the reader to decipher character motivations. Minimalism is also often associated with working-class characters, domestic subject matter, and marital dissolution, earning it the nickname “Kmart realism.”

The following stories are by writers associated with minimalism. The stories are as dense as diamonds, containing truth in very few words. As always, all are free to download.

“Nightschool” by Raymond Carver
A classic Raymond Carver setup: a divorcé narrator, a bar setting, and dialogue sparking with competing desires. We don’t know why the narrator’s wife left him, but we sense his desperation and alienation as he entertains a wild suggestion from two women who strike up a conversation with him at the Donner Club. An atmosphere of melancholy hangs over the encounter.

“Pretty Story” by Amy Hempel
Amy Hempel wrote her first story in a workshop led by Gordon Lish and has since become known for her miniaturist masterpieces. In this later story, a woman voices her anxieties about having a child: “And when I come out of the theatre, it occurs to me that it has been years since I have been to Paris. Years. So I go to Paris, and come back three months later and find a skeleton in the crib.”

“Trick Scenery” by Frederick Barthelme
Told from an off-kilter second-person perspective, Frederick Barthelme’s story follows a man with “a face like an old sack, like an old vegetable” as he takes a road trip, yearning for a woman to sit next to him. The story’s language is incantatory, with repetitions that echo the passing scenery. We know nothing about the man except his yearning.

“Solo Dance” by Jayne Anne Phillips
In this hyper-compressed story, Phillips depicts a woman visiting her father following his cancer operation. The family’s alienation and the father’s divorce from the narrator’s mother are revealed through asides. In a darkly comic turn, the father hopes to regain enough weight post-surgery to pummel his ex-wife’s divorce lawyer.

Weekly Newsletter

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

“Happy Boy, Allen” by Mary Robison
Mary Robison’s brand of minimalism features whip-smart dialogue and crystalline descriptions, including pillows “the color of Easter candy.” Young Allen visits his aunt to complain about his father remarrying after his mother’s death. The two get sloshed, but not before pontificating about painting, the nature of faces, and family resentments.

“Dancing” by Ann Beattie
In Beattie’s elegant story of marital dissolution, the narrator looks at a summer house with her ex-husband and his brother-in-law. Why is she there, helping her ex-husband buy a house she’ll never visit? She doesn’t seem to know, and we wonder alongside her. Unlike some of the other writers in the roundup, Beattie applies her minimalist vision to upper-middle-class life, “dissecting yuppies with precision,” according to a New York Times review.

items.title: The Chinese-Only Schools of the Jim Crow South
items.description:
A 1920s court battle over a Chinese American student exposed the complicated racial boundaries of school segregation.

The post The Chinese-Only Schools of the Jim Crow South appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
The initial court ruling seemed like a victory for Chinese Americans in the Mississippi Delta: Chinese children could attend school with their white peers, said the judge. But the Mississippi Circuit Court’s decision in the 1924 case was soon overturned.

The first judge had accepted that Chinese students should not have to share facilities with African Americans, whom he called “wholly different from them in racial characteristics.”

Yet the Supreme Court ultimately pointed to the state Constitution’s stipulation that “separate schools shall be maintained for children of the white and colored races.” And “[y]ellow, after all, was a color,” as educational researcher Sieglinde Lim de Sánchez remarks.

Decades before Mendez v. Westminster and the landmark Brown v. Board of Education, the case of Gong Lum, et al. v. Rice shows the ideological contradictions of school segregation.

When petitioner Gong Lum fought for his daughter to be admitted to a white school, his legal argument was that the Chinese should not be counted as “colored.”

Chinese immigrants came to the Delta as agricultural workers in the 1870s—soon forming family-centered rural enclaves that contrasted with the bachelor society of urban Chinatowns.

While they lived in predominantly African American areas, Mississippi Chinese “resisted legal and customary efforts to conflate their status with that of blacks” under Jim Crow laws—a sign of the unclear racial status of Southerners who were neither white nor African American.

Community leaders “consulted with sympathetic whites who urged them to adopt ‘white’ behavior patterns in their dealings with African Americans,” explains Lim de Sánchez.

When petitioner Gong Lum fought for his daughter to be admitted to a white school, his legal argument was that the Chinese should not be counted as “colored.”

“If a Chinese family lived in one of the smaller Delta town[s], and was good friends with the Bok Guey [whites], they’d let you go to their school,” longtime Delta resident Jack Chow recalled in an interview with Lim de Sánchez.

As Chinese parents began boarding their children with Rosedale families or moving into the district, the white townspeople of Rosedale pushed back—resulting in the court case that legally barred Chinese American students from accessing white-only schools.

Sending their children to segregated African American schools was out of the question for Chinese community leaders, who considered the matter “an issue of crucial importance.”

Instead, the Mississippi Chinese found a way to have schools of their own. Baptist congregations, eager to proselytize to the Chinese community, were already offering nighttime classes to teach adults English and encourage “Americanized” domestic habits.

“The Chinese gradually realized the missions could be crucial institutional vehicles in facilitating their drive toward full participation in white society, for they provided a forum to demonstrate to whites that they were not heathen,” Lim de Sánchez notes.

With Chinese parents’ backing, local Baptist churches opened various educational missions in the 1930s, including a single-story “shotgun shack” backed by the First Baptist Church of Greenville and a school under Rosedale Consolidated School’s Chinese Department.

More to Explore

Brown v. Board of Education: Annotated

Liz Tracey
May 17, 2023
The 1954 Supreme Court decision, based on the Fourteenth Amendment to the US Constitution, declared that “separate but equal” has no place in education.

One notable institution was the Cleveland Chinese Mission School, which opened in 1937 with donations from Chinese communities as far away as New York and San Francisco and even attracted out-of-state Chinese students from places like Tennessee and Arkansas.

Though Chinese community leaders supported after-school programs to impart Chinese culture, the schools were established mainly to teach English. They did not necessarily offer high-quality instruction—the Cleveland school was not even accredited by the state.

Still, mission schools allowed Mississippi Chinese to gain social acceptance in the racially segregated South, as they could “demonstrat[e] to whites that they possessed a cultural heritage and ‘innate’ capabilities that differed from African Americans.”

This came at the expense of Chinese Americans’ relationships with their African American neighbors, as they feared “any association might reverse the acceptance they had spent years trying to achieve within the larger Delta white society,” Lim de Sánchez says.

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

Interracial families were ostracized, and mixed-race children were excluded from the Baptist mission schools. Instead, they attended the local African American public or Catholic schools.

Eventually, Chinese parents in the Delta realized the limitations of a separate school system, and some opted to send their older children to public schools in other states—such as California and Texas—until white Delta schools began racial integration in the mid-1940s.

But recovering the pre–World War II history of these mission schools in the South is critical to “the formation and understanding of issues of educational segregation as well as racial inequality in the United States as a whole,” Lim de Sánchez concludes.

Despite the discrimination they faced, Mississippi Chinese “successfully established alternative schools that paralleled the exclusionary white educational institutions.”

items.title: Why Is Raja Ravi Varma’s Art So Valuable Today?
items.description:
A record-breaking auction spotlights the artist who transformed Hindu imagery and helped shape modern Indian visual culture.

The post Why Is Raja Ravi Varma’s Art So Valuable Today? appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
In April, a new record was set for the Indian art market when a painting by renowned Indian artist Raja Ravi Varma, created in the late nineteenth century, became the most expensive Indian artwork ever sold at auction. Yashoda and Krishna sold for 1.67 billion rupees ($17.9 million), far surpassing the previous record, held by modernist painter MF Husain’s Untitled (Gram Yatra), which sold for $13.8 million in 2025.

It’s noteworthy that an artwork painted in a predominantly Western-influenced style and depicting an overtly religious subject could command such a high price in a market where works by modernist artists have reigned for decades.

Professor Knut A. Jacobsen argues that Ravi Varma was the undisputed founder of a genre he terms the “God poster industry.”

Ravi Varma, born in 1848, belonged to the royal family of Travancore, a kingdom in what is now the southern Indian state of Kerala. He challenged caste and class hierarchies by choosing to be a painter and became the first Indian artist to paint Indian subjects in a Western style. He is widely regarded as a pioneer of modern Indian painting and one of the most influential artists from the subcontinent. Varma’s popularity grew at the height of the British Empire in India, as Western-style oil painting, with its emphasis on depth and chiaroscuro, gained prominence in the country. He began by painting grand portraits of royal and noble figures from across India and later turned to scenes from Hindu mythology in his work, becoming the first Indian artist to gain a nationwide audience.

In “Indian Painting from 1825 to 1900,” published in the 2011 volume Masters of Indian Painting II: 1650-1900, independent researcher Tryna Lyons describes Varma as “the first of India’s ‘gentleman artists’” because, “at the time that he made the daring decision to learn the craft of painting, artists enjoyed roughly the same social status as tailors and cabinet makers.”

By adopting the expensive medium of oil paint, Ravi Varma popularized the foreign art of representation, which, according to Lyons, was “primarily concerned with duplicating the observed world.” Yet it was his “theatrical interpretations of Sanskrit epic and drama” that glorified scenes from Hindu mythology and made him a household name.

His paintings and oleographs, produced by his own printing press, came to define Hindu religious iconography in India. Professor Knut A. Jacobsen, in his 2004 article, “The Child Manifestation of Śiva in Contemporary Hindu Popular Prints,” published in Numen, argues that Ravi Varma was the undisputed founder of a genre he terms the “God poster industry.” This genre took on a vibrant life of its own and remains popular today.

Jacobsen writes: “During the last one hundred years colourful prints of the Hindu gods, usually called God posters, have become one of the most visible aspects of popular religious culture in South Asia. There is hardly a Hindu home, shop or workshop without one print or more on the wall or on the puja table.”  He connects this popularity to sacred narratives, noting that “some of the posters do indeed illustrate sacred narratives found in the Saiva Puranas. The artists re-actualise themes from the Puranas.”

Despite his focus on Hindu religious iconography, Lyons argues that Ravi Varma also embraced the ideal of “harmony in diversity,” which came to define modern India. She cites his participation in the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago, where he displayed ten works featuring female subjects from across India in regional dress.

Anthropologist and art historian Christopher Pinney, however, offers a different interpretation in his 1997 article, “The Nation (Un)Pictured? Chromolithography and ‘Popular’ Politics in India, 1878–1995,” published in Critical Inquiry. He identifies the Ravi Varma Press as a main propagator of Hindu religious ideals and political ideas. He writes:

The ubiquity of Hindu propaganda is a necessary mark of the popularity of religious nationalism, and the proliferation and invasiveness of the imagery contriv[es] a sense of the irresistible tide of Hindutva … Both the Chitrashala Press and the Ravi Varma Press (which started in 1894) found themselves at the nexus of a political ferment in western and northern India. A diverse set of individuals and groups were involved in strategies which mobilised both two- and three-dimensional imagery in their attempts to control public spaces. In agitations such as that over Cow Protection and Tilak’s co-optation of the Ganpati festival, there was a less visible, but no less potent, colonisation of private domestic spaces by the products of early presses which ran parallel to the much better known struggles over public spaces and signs.

The “new media,” which included oleographs, captured the popular imagination in the early 1890s. British officials at the time saw this development as the emergence of “print nationalism.” Pinney argues that the female figures in Ravi Varma’s work helped drive its proliferation. He cites the painting Tarini, “in which it has been suggested an enveloping sari assumes the form of India (though curiously an India without Bengal). More than any other individual, Ravi Varma crystallized a putative Indian national identity in various feminine figures.”

Raja Ravi Varma’s iconic status in the Indian art pantheon is undeniable. However, the record-breaking sale raises a question: Why now? The high-value sale of his painting in 2026 may reflect the changing political landscape in India, where Hindutva politics has gained influence in recent years. After all, history repeats itself, and the popularity of historical art can, too.

items.title: A Brief History of Women’s Underwear
items.description:
The University of Wyoming’s Historic Clothing Collection offers a revealing look beneath the fashions of the past.

The post A Brief History of Women’s Underwear appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
The University of Wyoming is home to an archive of undergarments. And its collection of unmentionables—from the simple chemises of the Civil War era to the neon nylon stockings of the go-go years—is definitely worth talking about. In every stitch, there is a story.

The trove of women’s bloomers, drawers, knickers, brassieres, corsets, and girdles is just a small part of the school’s historic clothing collection, with images shared by the University of Wyoming Libraries via JSTOR. Taken together, the intimates trace a timeline of scientific innovation, societal progress, and sometimes surprising aesthetic choices.

White Chemise, ca. 1860. Click on the image to take a closer look.
Yellow Nylon Stockings from the 1960s. Click on the image to take a closer look.
Off-white Stockings, ca. 1900. Click on the image to take a closer look.
Black Stockings from the 1910s. Click on the image to take a closer look.
White Mesh Stockings from the 1920s. Click on the image to take a closer look.

Here you can step through history in stockings. While the Victorian woman who wore that white cotton chemise would have hidden her often-colorful stockings beneath enormous crinolines, offering the barest hint of ankle, the turn-of-the-century woman, in her narrower skirts, knew her shins would be on display when she lifted her hem slightly to climb stairs. Hers might be embroidered with delicate flowers. In the 1910s, hems rose a few inches higher—in a practical and patriotic response to the Great War—and opaque fine mesh styles in geometric patterns became popular. Less than a decade later, wide mesh stockings were a signature look for the flapper, with her skirts hemmed just below the knee.

The flapper style was as functional as it was scandalous; the holes that allowed skin to show through also gave the fabric the stretch necessary for dancing. In 1940 came the invention of nylon undergarments, which meant women of the midcentury could be more comfortable and less revealing in stockings that mimicked some skin tones. That they were followed by their younger sisters in bright, glittering stockings under miniskirts in the 1960s makes a lot more sense when you know what came before.

Peach Cami-Knickers from the 1920s. Click on the image to take a closer look.
Black Bloomers from the 1900s. Click on the image to take a closer look.
Undergarment Envelope Combination from the 1910s. Click on the image to take a closer look.
White Under-split Drawers from the 1890s. Click on the image to take a closer look.

In the collection, you can also see the literal foundations of women’s everyday lives through the decades. A pair of billowy, pleated black bloomers that would have looked a lot like drawers to earlier generations meant freedom to New Women of the 1900s, who bicycled and played sports in the once-scandalous attire. The 1910s envelope combination, a one-piece garment that combined the chemise and drawers, reshaped women’s lives, slimming down the stereotypical silhouette. In the 1920s, the envelope combination evolved into cami-knickers, the undergarment that would define the postwar Jazz Age. Loose, tube-shaped cami-knickers created the boyish shape favored by flappers, and silky, slinky fabrics like crepe de chine added modern allure to once-utilitarian pieces.

Expectations of women—and their underwear—changed yet again after the Second World War. In 1947, French fashion designer Christian Dior debuted a curvy, hourglass style that emphasized a full bust, cinched waist, and sloping hips. The designs were a backlash against the boxy, tailored uniforms of the war era and soon became known as the “New Look”—though any student of fashion history would have recognized the silhouette as a throwback to the previous century. With this new trend came a demand for all-in-one girdles, which shaped the body from bust to hips with elasticized panels and boning, and half slips, which continued the smooth illusion through the upper legs.

Browsing the virtual closets of the University of Wyoming, you can assemble an outfit piece by piece. Start with a green ruffled cocktail dress and a veiled black hat, then add a small black clutch and black stilettos designed by Palter DeLiso, until the full picture of a real woman and her story emerges from countless yards and yards of fabric.
