items.title: What Civics Class Is For
items.description:
Should schools tackle controversial political issues? A 1903 educator thought doing so was essential to preparing future voters.

The post What Civics Class Is For appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
For more than a century, Americans have commonly asked how public schools could do a better job of teaching people to be good citizens. One early stab at the question came from S. E. Forman, an early advocate for civics education. Writing in 1903, he noted that it was no surprise things hadn’t been ironed out yet, since the word civics “is only about fifteen years old and the thing is even younger.”

In marked contrast to today’s focus on school as training for future employment, Forman wrote that “we are told in season and out of season” that training for good citizenship “is the chief function of the school.”

Forman was distressed to find that civics teachers often avoided looking at specific political issues of the day, judging them to be too controversial.

Forman argued that civics should begin by encouraging students to “think as much as possible about democracy.” This included understanding the history of democratic ideas and practical governance, as well as the need to protect minority groups and the dangers posed by demagogues.

Along with understanding the “spirit” of democracy, he wrote, students should understand its principles, including federalism, checks and balances, and civil liberty. He also noted the need to teach how the US government is organized, including the workings of various bodies at the local, state, and national levels. However, he argued that the civics classes of his time were altogether too focused on the mechanical aspects of governance, much to the dismay of students.

“In the acquisition of this knowledge they come to look upon civics as the driest, the most unprofitable, and the most stupid of all their studies,” Forman wrote. “And their impressions are often just.”

More to Explore

The Case for Lowering the Voting Age

Livia Gershon
October 17, 2018
If the standard we hold for who can vote is the consent of the governed, why shouldn’t children be included?

Forman was also distressed to find that civics teachers often avoided looking at specific political issues of the day, judging them to be too controversial. He suggested that this was a mistake and that it’s crucial for students to understand the topics that will come before them as voters.

He praised one high school teacher he had watched present a lesson on tariffs. At the time, this was a key issue in a presidential election. While the class was divided between protectionists and free-traders, the teacher gave no indication of his own views, and the textbook presented objective facts along with arguments from both sides. The point, Forman suggested, was not to change anyone’s mind but to encourage better understanding and clearer thinking.

Finally, Forman argued that civics must touch on ethics, but without leaning on religious arguments inappropriate for the classroom. Instead, he viewed teachers’ own moral values, conduct, and character as key to presenting students with a model of decency.

“To vote right requires a happy union of head and heart,” he wrote. “And if instruction in civics does not effect this union, as likely as not its chief result will be to prepare many of the learners for more successful and intelligent careers as public rogues.”

items.title: The Jewish Labor Bund’s Anti-Zionist Legacy
items.description:
For many Jewish leftists before 1948, Zionism was far from the only vision for the Jewish future.

The post The Jewish Labor Bund’s Anti-Zionist Legacy appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Molly Crabapple’s new best-seller, Here Where We Live is Our Country: The Story of the Jewish Labor Bund tells the nearly lost history of the “most influential Jewish political force in eastern Europe.” In the first two decades of the twentieth century, the General Jewish Labor Bund in Lithuania, Poland, and Russia—the places where the majority of Jews in the world then lived—was secular, socialist, and “uncompromisingly anti-Zionist.”

Zionism, the movement for a “Jewish homeland,” was antithetical to the Bundists’ sense of community, doikayt (Yiddish for “hereness”), succinctly summarized in Crabapple’s title: here where we live is our country. Migration to a thereness, or dorkayt, in the Middle East was the wrong path in the eyes of Bundists. The Bund was formed in 1897, the same year the First Zionist Congress was held to begin the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine.

During the “red decade” of the 1930s, more Jews passed through membership in the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) than through the liberal American Jewish Committee.

This history complicates the contemporary argument that anti-Zionism is necessarily antisemitic: some Jewish political movements, including the Bund, were themselves explicitly anti-Zionist.

The Bund didn’t survive Hitler and Stalin, but its legacy lived on, particularly among Eastern European Jews who migrated to the United States before the racially discriminatory national origins immigration quotas of 1924. Cultural studies scholar Benjamin Balthaser takes up the Jewish anti-Zionist legacy in Citizens of the Whole World: Anti-Zionism and the Cultures of the American Jewish Left. For the Bund, writes Balthaser in American Quarterly:

Zionism’s “separatist, chauvinist, clerical, and conservative” culture was understood as the “polar opposite” of the radical Yiddish-speaking organizations of Europe that were progressive, secular, and internationalist.

American Jews between the world wars were predominantly working class and left-wing. Balthaser describes how they were despised by the dominant Protestant culture as a “biopolitical” threat, the “most racially alien” and “unassimilable” of immigrants. Balthaser also notes that during the “red decade” of the 1930s, more Jews passed through membership in the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) than through the liberal American Jewish Committee. For these Jews, calls for the creation of a new Zion was petit-bourgeois, right-wing nationalist, and imperialist, “directly or indirectly requiring the support of the British Empire.”

For Jewish communists, the promised land was communism, not what the CPUSA called the “Jim Crowism” of Jewish-only settlements.

More to Explore

The Editors
October 19, 2023

Even the resolutely non-communist Hannah Arendt, as late as 1945, saw Zionism as an elite collaboration with European imperialism that would “pass over” the “genuine national revolutionary movement which sprang from the Jewish masses.”

In 1947, the Soviet Union, writes Balthaser, “which had either sided with Palestinian anti-colonial revolts or at least was ambiguous enough so that local and national Communist Parties often went their own way,” came out in support of Partition. This was the UN plan to split British Mandate Palestine into Arab and Jewish states. Followers of the Moscow “line” suddenly switched from “advocating a binational, democratic state to supporting a single Jewish state.”

The 1948 Arab–Israeli War culminated in the establishment of Israel and the expulsion of nearly 700,000 Palestinians from their homes. Balthaser connects that history to what he describes as decades of Palestinian “displacement and state violence” and, since 1967, Israel’s “settler colonial project.”

For Balthaser, these developments bore out some of the Jewish left’s warnings about Zionism as a project of nationalism, imperialism, and ethnic exclusion. He argues that the “wide-spread opposition of working-class and left-wing US Jews to Zionism during the 1930s and most of the 1940s” was largely forgotten in the following decades as Zionism was claimed to “represent the unified interests or will of ‘the Jewish people.’”

But the legacy of Jewish anti-Zionism has been reawakened in the work cited here, and in the writings of Peter Beinart, Judith Butler, Naomi Klein, Shaul Magid, and others, as well as, more collectively, in organizations like Jewish Voice for Peace, IfNotNow, and a reborn Jewish Labor Bund.

items.title: Why Is Leadership Riskier for Women?
items.description:
Research shows that harsher penalties for failure can discourage women from pursuing top positions.

The post Why Is Leadership Riskier for Women? appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Two competing theories are frequently offered to explain why women are dramatically underrepresented in the highest leadership positions, from Congress to Fortune 500 companies. Some argue that cultural norms of male leadership and even outright discrimination keep women from top roles, while others argue that women are less ambitious than men. These explanations may not be mutually exclusive, though. Research by Susan R. Fisk and Jon Overton shows that women’s leadership ambitions are depressed by the expectation that women will be disproportionately penalized for failures.

Fisk and Overton use three surveys to trace how expectations of harsher penalties for failure can dampen women’s leadership ambitions. First, they find that both women and men—but women to a greater degree—”believe that women leaders face greater sanctions for failure than otherwise similar men.” There’s good reason for that belief. Research has found, for example, that “women managers are formally penalized more harshly for committing an ethical violation than otherwise similar men managers” and “women surgeons receive a sharper drop in referrals when a patient dies than male surgeons.” Fisk and Overton’s findings suggest that this phenomenon is common knowledge.

Harsher sanctions for women leaders when things go wrong can discourage women from seeking those roles in the first place.

Second, they asked respondents to consider whether they would take on a professional leadership role with a high risk of failure. Half of the respondents were told that failure would not affect their careers: they could return to their current team and could count on support from their manager. The other half were told that failure could mean losing their job and that their manager had not pledged support. Both men and women were less likely to say they wanted the leadership role when failure carried these risks—but the effect was stronger for women.

Laura Clawson
February 20, 2026
A study of employment discrimination cases reveals how bias operates through workplace rules.

The final study used the same scenario as the second, but added additional controls and questions to test whether women’s lower interest in a risky leadership role could be linked to their expectation of greater sanctions for failure—and to rule out alternative explanations. The research found that “anticipated sanctions account for about 31 percent of the decrease in women’s leadership ambitions.”

It is true, then, that women can be less likely than men to have leadership ambitions. But that is not simply an innate difference. Rather, to a significant extent, it can be a response to the greater risk women face in leadership positions. As a result, harsher sanctions for women leaders when things go wrong can discourage women from seeking those roles in the first place. As Fisk and Overton write, “gender discrimination against women leaders not only harms women leaders: this discrimination also decreases the likelihood that women pursue leadership positions in the first place.”

items.title: How Kudzu Was Supposed to Save the South
items.description:
Before it became a notorious invasive plant, kudzu was promoted as a solution to widespread soil erosion.

The post How Kudzu Was Supposed to Save the South appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Across the American South, few plants are as recognizable as kudzu. Its vines blanket trees and power lines, turning roadside clearings into walls of green. Over time, this landscape has given rise to the story of a “vine that ate the South,” with kudzu framed as a menacing invader that swallows everything in its path. But kudzu’s presence in the South is more complicated than this myth suggests. Brought to the region to address economic and environmental woes shaped by the ghost of plantation slavery, kudzu was later abandoned as shifting needs rendered the plant unnecessary. Though its purported usefulness was short-lived, kudzu has persisted in both the landscape and the collective memory of the South.

Kudzu (Pueraria montana) is a perennial climbing vine native to East Asia, particularly China and Japan. It has broad leaves, organized in groups of three, and large, tuberous roots, which allow the plant to survive and regenerate even after its aboveground growth is removed. Under favorable conditions with plenty of rainfall and mild winters, Pueraria montana can grow as much as sixty feet in a season, with some reports alleging that its vines may extend by roughly twelve inches in a single day during periods of rapid growth. Kudzu also fixes nitrogen through its symbiotic relationship with soil bacteria, allowing it to thrive in nutrient-poor or heavily disturbed soils. It is especially successful in sunny, open environments, such as forest edges, roadsides, and abandoned fields. As a result, kudzu is exceptionally skilled at flourishing in damaged landscapes.

Decades of land abuse and exploitation left behind a scarred terrain uniquely prepared for the arrival of kudzu as a fast-growing pioneer plant.

Kudzu’s characteristics made it well suited to thrive in the southeastern United States. The plantation economy that developed in the American South institutionalized an intensely extractive relationship with the land. As historian David Silkenat argues in his book Scars on the Land: An Environmental History of Slavery in the American South, Southern planters prioritized maximizing production through enslaved labor rather than sustaining the health and long-term productivity of the land. The result was a landscape repeatedly cleared and exhausted for cotton and other cash crops.

By the twentieth century, intensive farming practices had left the South dangerously vulnerable to erosion, producing depleted swaths of land where kudzu would later flourish. Kurt Kinbacher traces this history to an enduring American assumption that land was essentially limitless, citing a 1909 Bureau of Soils declaration that “soil is one indestructible, immutable asset that the nation possesses” and “the one resource that cannot be exhausted; that cannot be used up.” In reality, decades of land abuse and exploitation left behind a scarred terrain uniquely prepared for the arrival of kudzu as a fast-growing pioneer plant.

The vine made its American debut as an exotic plant at the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition in 1876, where it was displayed as part of the Japanese government’s exhibition and first caught the attention of American gardeners. Seven years later, kudzu was brought to the South as part of the New Orleans Exposition, where Southern gardeners took notice of its potential as an attractive ornamental vine they could use to provide much-needed shade for porches and gardens. By the early 1900s, pioneering farmer C. E. Pleas had begun experimenting with the vine as feed for his livestock in Florida, but by 1934, only about 10,000 acres of kudzu had been planted across the nation.

Amid the crises of the Great Depression and mass soil erosion that devastated agricultural production, the United States began to view kudzu as a “miracle vine” with the potential to save the South. In 1933, Congress established the Soil Erosion Service, which was later renamed the Soil Conservation Service and eventually became the Natural Resources Conservation Service.

More to Explore

Kari Traylor
June 25, 2026
The tangled history of an invasive plant and a scientist’s troubling quest to engineer a more efficient natural world.

The creation of this federal program helped spur a rapid expansion of kudzu across the South. Between 1935 and 1942, federal nurseries distributed over 85 million kudzu seedlings to Southern landowners, and the government offered farmers up to $8 per acre to plant the vine on their land. The newly established Civilian Conservation Corps also planted kudzu seedlings along deforested roadsides, which were particularly vulnerable to soil erosion. Popular enthusiasm grew alongside government support, driven in part by figures such as Georgia journalist and radio show host Channing Cope, who created the “Kudzu Club of America” and championed the vine as the region’s economic savior. By 1946, approximately 3 million acres of kudzu had been planted on farmland across the Southeast.

At the time, the strategy appeared successful. One study conducted at the Soil Conservation Service’s experiment station at Watkinsville, Georgia, found that “land under kudzu had nearly 80 percent less water runoff and over 99percent less soil loss than land under cotton.” Kudzu seemed to offer exactly what the South needed: a fast-growing, inexpensive plant that reinvigorated depleted Southern soil while producing a useful crop.

But as post-WWII agriculture shifted toward chemical fertilizers, herbicides, and heavy machinery, the need for kudzu decreased rapidly, and the federal government retracted its support for the crop. In 1953, the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) removed kudzu from its list of cover plants permissible under the Agricultural Conservation Program. By 1962, the Soil Conservation Service had reversed its earlier support, recommending that the vine only be planted far from developed areas. In 1972, the USDA listed kudzu as a common weed in the South, and in 1997, it was added to the Federal Noxious Weed List, effectively prohibiting the interstate transport of kudzu without approval from the Secretary of Agriculture.

Federal abandonment of kudzu left the plant to spread along the unmanaged margins of the region, sparking exaggerated fears about its unchecked growth. Popular media and Southern folklore frequently claimed that kudzu was swallowing 150,000 new acres every year and had overtaken anywhere from 7 to 9 million acres across the region. According to naturalist Bill Finch, kudzu’s threat to Southern landscapes has been exaggerated. Finch argues that because kudzu is most aggressive along roads, railways, and forest edges, the vine has become hyper-visible in the age of the automobile. In reality, Finch notes that the reach of the sun-loving vines does not extend far beyond these brightly lit edge habitats. Data from the Forest Service tentatively confirms Finch’s hypothesis, suggesting that kudzu occupies around 227,000 acres of Southern land, just a small fraction of the millions of acres it has been said to cover.

The dramatic gap between public perception and ecological reality reveals how deeply kudzu has become embedded in Southern memory. For generations of Southerners, the vine has been a familiar feature of roadsides and rural landscapes. Writers have used it to evoke Southern identity and decline, while others have looked to the plant as a symbol of the region’s stubborn resilience. As Derek H. Alderman and Donna G. Alderman argue, people use kudzu as a metaphor for a range of social and environmental issues, and the plant has become a cultural lens through which Southerners understand environmental threats beyond the vine itself.

Kudzu’s reputation, then, tells us as much about the changing South as it does about the plant itself. Its shifting roles show how human needs can reshape the meaning and understanding of a plant. The Plant Humanities Initiative at Dumbarton Oaks asks us to consider precisely these entangled relationships between plants and people, prompting us to examine the many meanings that grow around them.

items.title: Not All Boredom Is the Same
items.description:
Psychology suggests that boredom is a signal. Understanding its cause can help us decide how to respond.

The post Not All Boredom Is the Same appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Boredom is a fact of everyday life. It may strike when we’re reading a dry philosophy text, watching a Disney movie with our kids for the millionth time, or filling out repetitive paperwork. Psychology researcher Erin C. Westgate argues that boredom, like pain, is a signal that something has gone wrong. But what we should do about it depends on what kind of boredom we’re talking about.

Westgate outlines the meaning-and-attentional components (MAC) model of boredom. As the name suggests, it presents boredom as having two kinds of sources. We can get bored when the thing we’re doing feels like it has no salient goal or meaning, or when we simply can’t pay attention.

If boredom is caused by meaninglessness, it may help to adjust our mental model of our goals.

That second type, attentional boredom, involves the alignment between our cognitive capacity and the task at hand. When these are well aligned, it could look like energetically tackling a tricky work assignment, or relaxing after a long day by watching a formulaic sitcom. In contrast, we might get bored either by watching the sitcom when we’re ready for a challenge or by trying to do the hard task when we’re already drained.

In experiments, Westgate and her colleagues have found that attention and meaning are independent predictors of boredom—we get bored if either is missing. Attentional boredom tends to cause mind wandering and sometimes agitation and frustration. Meaningless boredom is more likely to result in sadness, loneliness, a sense that time is dragging, and a desire to disengage. It’s also possible to experience mixed boredom, when both attention and meaning are lacking.

Depending on what’s causing boredom, Westgate offers several types of action we might take to respond to the signal it’s sending us:

  • Regulate cognitive demands: To improve our ability to pay attention, we might make a task easier—perhaps by breaking it into smaller pieces—or harder—for example, by setting a timer and working as fast as possible.
  • Regulate cognitive resources: To improve the mental energy we bring to a task that’s a bit too demanding, we might get better sleep, drink caffeine, or, in the longer term, get more practice. Conversely, Westgate notes that a time-honored, if suboptimal, solution for understimulation is reducing one’s cognitive capacity by drinking on the job.
  • Regulate goal value: If boredom is caused by meaninglessness, it may help to adjust our mental model of our goals. For example, students may be able to better focus on a task if they see how it contributes to their long-term educational objectives.
  • Switch activities: In some cases, the best choice may be to find something different to do. If you’re understimulated or feeling a sense that your task has no meaning, it may help to seek more novelty and complexity. If you’re bored because a task is too hard, it may be more appealing to find something easy and enjoyable. However, doing that on a regular basis may mean engaging in less of the cognitive work that can help build more capacity, leading to greater boredom in the long run.

So when boredom strikes, the first question may not be how to get rid of it, but why it’s happening in the first place.

items.title: The Logistics That Powered the Vietnam War
items.description:
The Vietnam War became a testing ground for private contractors and military systems that still shape conflict today.

The post The Logistics That Powered the Vietnam War appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
The American war in Vietnam (1955–1975) is not typically viewed from the perspective of infrastructural power and the logistics of empire. But, as geographer Wesley Attewell argues, the war “catalyzed a revolution in imperial logistics,” requiring enormous transpacific flows of commodities and bodies, living and dead.

“Many of the specific technologies and calculative practices—just-in-time systems, containerization, and the like—that are now synonymous with logistics were first developed by the US military during World War II,” continues Attewell. But Vietnam saw more than just refinement of such logistical reach and power—it was a combat-contextual “stress-test” of “a deep hybridization of military and market methods” for “waging war across transnational space.”

One American general likened the buildup to the transportation of an entire American city across 10,000 miles.

As an example, the first automated, computerized “transportation command and control system of its kind” was developed as the US ramped up military involvement in 1965. That was the first year combat troops—as opposed to “military advisors”—were deployed. Some 3,500 Marines arrived in early March; six months later the combat force would stand at some 125,000. Three years later, in 1968, a peak of 536,100 troops was reached. One American general likened the buildup to the transportation of an entire American city across 10,000 miles.

Long before the militarized subcontracting of the Gulf Wars became a scandal, Vietnam witnessed the first private contract in an active theater of war. A consortium of four companies, operating as Raymond Morrison Knudsen-Brown and Root and Jones (RMK-BRJ), handled what was then the largest construction project in the world. They constructed enormous “logistics islands” of defensible airfields, deep-water ports, and distribution complexes. In addition to the military material, the delivery of commercial goods from the US Agency for International Development (USAID) made for very crowded facilities.

More to Explore

The Birth of the Modern American Military Hospital

Julia Métraux
May 29, 2023
The founding of Walter Reed General Hospital at the beginning of the twentieth century marked a shift in medical care for military personnel and veterans.

(Texas-based Brown and Root was a major backer of the political career of Lyndon Johnson, the president who exponentially increased the US presence in Vietnam. Brown and Root later became a subsidiary of Halliburton, whose former CEO, Dick Cheney, was Vice President of the US from 2001–2009.)

RMK-BRJ also hired both unskilled locals and more specialized “Third-Country Nationals”( TCNs), mostly from South Korea and the Philippines. As subcontractors, these workers were outside the purview and responsibility of the US and its military.

“What emerged was a familiar hierarchy of racialized labor, which ranked white workers above South Koreans and Filipinxs, who were themselves deemed more ‘advanced’ than the Vietnamese,” writes Attewell. Collective action was thus intentionally undermined. Nonetheless, antagonisms between the groups and their treatment by Americans resulted in a “militant politics of resistance, rooted in a dynamic geography of strikes, blockades, and walkouts.” Racially stereotyped as “docile and malleable,” these workers were anything but. Such “friction” in the logistical gears has not been represented in American portrayals of the war.

Attewell gives some examples of the labor problems. In 1966, 129 militant women dockers were fired by RMK-BRJ, one of the factors that led to a Saigon dock strike at the end of that year. A protest over the food served to South Koreans at the Cam Ranh Bay complex turned violent in late 1967. The “hardcore troublemakers” were sent home to Korea, which, as a source of recruitment, also saw its share of labor unrest over jobs in Vietnam. Conflicts at Newport, a small dock a couple of miles from the center of Saigon that was massively upscaled to a deepwater facility between 1965–1967, made for another “cauldron of logistical friction.” A 1971 strike at Newport reduced daily port operations by three-fourths.

Vietnamese labor unions were in the thick of it, both blessed by the largess and cursed by the exploitative system. Infrastructure was also gendered, with Vietnamese women “meant to satisfy the ‘private’ needs—food, care, intimacy, and sex—of US soldiers.” Attewell notes that “maids were just as militant as dockers, truckers, or warehouse workers.”

Conditions changed with waning US involvement in the early 1970s, although here too conflict arose. When the 12-hour dockyard shifts were reduced to 10-hour, workers felt their already precarious standards of living threatened.

When the North Vietnamese overran Saigon at the end of April 1975, the infrastructure left behind by the US was a sprawling complex of facilities, acres of concrete, stockpiles of weapons, pervasive toxic pollution—and abandoned allies, including the TCNs.

items.title: Why Hawaii Put Japanese into Public Schools
items.description:
Political and religious leaders battled for influence through the education of Japanese immigrant children.

The post Why Hawaii Put Japanese into Public Schools appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
When Honolulu’s McKinley High School began offering Japanese language classes in 1924, the program wasn’t introduced only to accommodate the needs of migrant workers’ children. The curriculum—a first for the local public school system—was also a bid to control communal loyalties in Hawaii, which the United States had annexed in 1898.

“[C]onflict over religion and assimilation seems to have been the motivation behind making Japanese part of the secondary curricula in Hawaii public schools,” explains Noriko Asato, an archive specialist whose research focuses on Japanese American history. Japanese laborers had been migrating to Hawaii since the 1890s, mainly to work on sugar plantations. Even though public schooling became compulsory in 1896, the language barrier and the remote location of many plantations led to gaps in access to these laborers’ formal education.

Japanese Christian leaders were quick to establish independent schools that offered a Japanese-style curriculum in the afternoons.

Eager to remedy this social problem, Japanese Christian leaders were quick to establish independent schools that offered a Japanese-style curriculum in the afternoons. The Christian missionaries who established these schools in the 1890s saw education as a way to improve the perception of their religion, which had been proscribed for centuries in Japan, as well as an opportunity to win converts from the mainly Buddhist Japanese community.

Buddhist clergy quickly responded—opening schools in Hilo and Kona in 1898 and in Honolulu in 1902, and sparking a showdown between leaders of both religions. “As competition between religious sects became more intense, it involved the entire Japanese community… prompting some parents to establish secular schools,” Asato writes.

By 1909, unaffiliated schools made up more than two-fifths of all Japanese language schools. Besides concerns over indoctrination, parents supported independent schools because the growth of religious schools “caus[ed] an enormous financial burden on the immigrant community,” which was expected to fund these institutions, she explains.

Tension around the role of religion in these schools was matched by a clash between the Japanese community and the white business and political elite in Hawaii. Plantation owners initially threw their weight behind temples, churches and schools as “incentives for laborers to settle,” as Asato puts it, and saw Buddhist Bishop Yemyо̄ Imamura’s intervention in a strike in 1904 as proof that Buddhism yielded compliant workers.

On the other hand, the Christian Hawaiian Evangelical Association sought to curtail its Buddhist rivals by telling the Department of Public Instruction that Buddhist schools “opposed the Americanism that Hawaii’s public schools had been nurturing,” Asato writes.

More to Explore

How Public Schools “Americanized” Hawai‘i

Livia Gershon
February 3, 2020
Colonial education administrators recruited teachers from the mainland, but soon realized another strategy was in order.

Representatives of the Japanese government were also drawn into the controversy. Despite Education Vice-Minister Seitarо̄ Sawayanagi’s mandate that overseas education promote Japanese values, local diplomats like the Honolulu consul general “often deliberately ignored Sawayanagi’s 1906 order whenever they encountered resistance.”

After all, opposition to Japanese language schools was mounting among the American public. “Many white public school teachers claimed they felt threatened to see the majority of their students ‘move’ to a nearby Japanese language school right after public school hours, where they imagined alien teachers subverted their democratic lessons,” Asato explains.

The Hawaii Japanese Education Association was formed in 1915 to allay these concerns. The group revised the Japanese syllabus to include pro-American content, including a textbook chapter that told students: “Future American citizens, do not bring a stain upon the name of the fatherland and do not disgrace your ancestor’s name.”

Yet these efforts were not enough to stave off a broader American campaign against all foreign language schools—including Japanese schools, which one report in 1920 characterized as “centers of an influence which, if not distinctly anti-American, is certainly un-American.”

Aiming to counter Buddhists’ influence in the community, Japanese Christians appealed to this nativist sentiment. Their push to move Japanese language lessons into the public school system succeeded, leading to inaugural classes at McKinley High in 1924 and Maui High in 1925.

All the same, language schools continued to hold their own, with more than 200 institutions enrolling more than 40,000 students in 1940. Only when war between the United States and Japan broke out the next year were Japanese schools in Hawaii forcibly closed.

Thankfully, “foreign language” education has since made a comeback. Japanese is now studied by tens of thousands of American schoolchildren—especially in California, Oregon, Washington and Hawaii, states with larger Japanese American populations. “[S]tudying the history of Japanese language schools in Hawaii,” writes Asato, “should contribute historical depth to Japanese language studies by elucidating our long and complex origins as providers of foreign and/or heritage language education.”

items.title: The Culture Wars of The Phantom of the Opera
items.description:
The hit musical became a battleground for competing ideas about capitalism, artistic value, and commercial theater.

The post The Culture Wars of The Phantom of the Opera appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
When it premiered in London in 1986 and expanded to Broadway two years later, Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Phantom of the Opera was not just a blockbuster thanks to its Gothic plot, operatic score, and the star power of its main cast (Sarah Brightman and Michael Crawford, who originated the roles of Christine and the Phantom for both runs), as well as Andrew Lloyd Webber himself. Rather, it became a leading subject of what we would now call “a culture war” over political, artistic, and cultural-historical questions.

Notably, the musical was reflective of the politics of the Thatcher and Reagan era, and by virtue of being the work of an English composer, it was also the latest entry in a wave of non-US productions threatening the supremacy of Broadway-native musicals and plays. When it opened on Broadway in 1988, it joined Starlight Express, Cats, Me and My Girl, and Les Misérables in the ranks of non-US productions dominating the Broadway lineup. As a result, when it premiered, parochialism-driven vitriol was expected on the US side. However, “It is too simplistic to suggest that British reviewers were uniformly supportive of Lloyd Webber and that Americans were uniformly hostile,” writes Amanda Eubanks Winkler in Cambridge Opera Journal. “Issues of politics, economics, taste and class implicitly or explicitly shaped the critical response to Phantom on both sides of the pond.”

“Webber’s financial success, his role as a player in the capitalist system, was entirely incompatible with true artistry.”

In the first place, Andrew Lloyd Webber was a noted conservative. “Lloyd Webber’s political affiliation was already well known in the mid-1980s, around the time of Phantom‘s premiere, as the composer had become a vocal advocate for Tory policy, particularly tax reform,” explains Winkler. “He also deployed his compositional gifts to serve the Conservative cause: in 1987, for instance, he provided music for Margaret Thatcher’s Party Election Broadcast to accompany a montage of Thatcher meeting with world leaders and engaging in other acts of statesmanship.” By 1988, when Phantom debuted on Broadway, the Reagan-era consumer culture and flashy opulence were on their way out, so the ornate, maximalist sets and the lush orchestrations felt off-key to reviewers. Using a review by pianist John Eaton in The Washington Post as a starting point, Winkler reflects on how “Webber’s financial success, his role as a player in the capitalist system, was entirely incompatible with true artistry—a rebuke against Reagan’s economic policies that sought to commodify the arts and saw little value in public subsidy.”

Commercially, the production was a success from day one, but outlets like The Village Voice chalked its popularity up to the middlebrow tastes of its audience, “implicat[ing] the artistically ignorant bourgeois consumers who made Phantom a hit,” writes Winkler.

By contrast, the UK press, especially conservative and Thatcher-adjacent outlets (including The Daily Express, The Daily Mail, and The Daily Telegraph), was largely supportive of Webber’s success, often serving as its de facto cheerleader, with criticisms directed at New York Times critics and headlines like “How Brits Keep Broadway in Business.”

“Certainly Lloyd Webber’s string of successful shows in the 1980s could be seen (and was seen by Thatcher) as triumphant exemplars of her free market philosophy,” writes Winkler.

The Financial Times went so far as to call Webber a “romantic, operatic composer,” a description that reflects the cultural debate that Phantom embodied and exemplified.

More to Explore

The Hidden Grief of American Musicals

Tim Brinkhof
July 8, 2026
Musicology professor Jake Johnson argues that beneath the bright songs and happy endings of midcentury musicals lay the grief and anxieties of postwar America.

Phantom also engaged with traditional art forms. “This is a work that foregrounds a dialogue with the past. It features an operatic, lushly orchestrated, almost through-sung score, and music heavily outweighs spoken dialogue during its two-and-a-half-hour run time,” writes Winkler. The individual songs also reference earlier music traditions: Carlotta’s “Prima Donna” is reminiscent of a Straussian waltz; Phantom’s own in-universe opera, Don Juan Triumphant, nods to Mozart’s precedent while also adopting a more modernist sound; and other tracks draw inspiration from Benjamin Britten and Meyerbeer. And as Winkler notes, “one can plausibly hear Phantom as a commercial repackaging of the past, a synthesis of the twin Thatcherite values of traditionalism and capitalism.” These references to opera and classical music did not carry a markedly political tone. Opera was largely perceived as elitist at the time, making it an uneasy fit with the populist rhetoric of 1980s conservatism, so Webber’s references to the repertory could be seen as a way to bridge the gap between past and present while also making a case for opera’s continued importance. Phantom’s operatic elements “may be more sophisticated than Oklahoma! and South Pacific,” argues Winkler, citing a panel of music critics and performers convened by The New York Times.

The divide in how audiences and critics received these operatic references was straightforward. For those who enjoyed Phantom‘s music, “Lloyd Webber’s adoption of an operatic idiom was a comforting sign that ‘high’ culture could survive without government subsidy in Reagan/Thatcher’s unforgiving commercial marketplace, and that broad audiences might still derive pleasure from the music of a latter-day Puccini,” writes Winkler. By contrast, for those who did not, “It was precisely Lloyd Webber’s commercialism (associated with the unbridled capitalism of the Reagan/Thatcher era) and the score’s accessibility and popular appeal that were so problematic.”

Ultimately, this debate served as a time capsule of the 1980s musical scene. Starting in the following decade, megamusicals such as Webber’s most notable productions declined in both commercial and critical success, giving way to jukebox musicals, musical adaptations of Disney classics, and irreverent subversions of the genre.

items.title: Where Did All the Public Bathrooms Go?
items.description:
Nineteenth-century Paris tackled public urination with ornate pissoirs. American reformers later turned toilets into a temperance cause.

The post Where Did All the Public Bathrooms Go? appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Here’s a pop quiz for you: What purpose did this little kiosk serve?

It’s quite a pretty little building—note the delicate grilles, the ornately etched glass, and the little bouquet of metal flowers bursting from the roof.

But of course, there is one key clue missing from the photograph: the smell. Or rather, the stench. This was one of Paris’s infamous public urinals—a pissoir (or vespasienne, if you’re inclined to be polite).

There was a moment around the mid-1800s in Paris when public urination began to be treated as a public health issue. A series of devastating cholera outbreaks led people to begin regarding human waste as a danger rather than a mere nuisance. Something had to be done.

Pissoirs looked like little palaces, crusted with iron flowers, shells, and scrolls—even, in some cases, tiny lions’ heads, glaring out as if to guard your back while you’re in the booth.

Before that point, authorities had installed empeche pipi here and there—a kind of hostile architecture meant to prevent rogue peeing. This might take the form of a row of iron spikes blocking an enticing corner, or a piece of bullnose masonry meant to send the stream shooting back onto the offender’s shoes.

The most these interventions could do was shunt prospective pee-ers from one spot to another. But, in 1850, public urination was actually banned. People were going to need somewhere to go.

Enter the pissoir. When you can’t smell them, it’s easy to wish they were still around. Nowadays, public restrooms are utilitarian at best, but these looked like little palaces, crusted with iron flowers, shells, and scrolls—even, in some cases, tiny lions’ heads, glaring out as if to guard your back while you’re in the booth. On the other hand, the greatest concession most of them made to privacy was a little iron screen separating the user from the street.

Enclosed six-stall urinal, Jardin de la Bourse, Place de la Bourse, 2nd arrondissement, Paris, circa 1865, via Wikimedia Commons
Single stall urinal with raised modesty screen, Square des Batignolles, Paris, circa 1865, via Wikimedia Commons
Slate cubicle with two stalls and doors, on curb of footpath, Place du Louvre, Paris, circa 1865, via Wikimedia Commons
Cast iron urinal with lamp post and lantern, Paris, 1876, via Wikimedia Commons
Single stall masonry urinal mounted with globe and advertising on sides, circa 1865, via Wikimedia Commons
Eight-stall urinal, cast iron and slate with shrubbery screen, Champs-Élysées Gardens, in front of the Palais de l'Industrie, 8th arrondissement, Paris, circa 1873, via Wikimedia Commons
Cast iron urinal on curb of street, advertising on panels of urinal walls, Paris, circa 1865, via Wikimedia Commons

Some were surmounted by glowing streetlamps, which served the joint purpose of making them easy to find and illuminating the advertisements with which they were liberally pasted. (Apparently, the perfumers and winemakers weren’t worried about unsavory associations with their product.)

Notably, they were only intended for use by men. The assumption was that women weren’t really much of a part of public life, and so wouldn’t need a way to relieve themselves while out on the street—kind of a self-fulfilling prophecy, if you think about it.

There was another use for the pissoir, which took their designers quite by surprise. Almost immediately, they became the favored meeting spot for men seeking rendezvous with one another. They were relatively private, secluded, and perfect for communicating anonymously with graffiti—the ideal release valve for a population that was prohibited from meeting publicly.

More to Explore

Early Doctors Diagnosed Disease by Looking at Urine

Morgan Godvin
March 24, 2023
When uroscopy became trendy, it caused a minor scandal within the early medical profession.

In “Dirty Desire: The Uses and Misuses of Public Urinals in Nineteenth-Century Paris” sociologist Andrew Israel Ross tracks the contested terrain of the urinal, writing:

[T]he case of the public urinals ultimately shows that the meaning of modern urban life emerged in a constantly shifting dialogue between those who conceived and built the city and those who ultimately used it. The tendency of the built environment to exceed the control of those who conceived it … is a distinguishing feature of modern urban life.

The crackdown followed swiftly. The police started patrolling particularly popular urinals. So did blackmailers, for whom merely stepping into a urinal was enough to launch a harassment campaign.

Meanwhile, in the United States, toilets were becoming a centerpiece in yet another hot-button issue: temperance. In the absence of other options, saloons had become the de facto public bathroom network for most major cities—which meant that anyone who needed to empty their bladder was regularly exposed to the enticements of drink.

As historian Peter C. Baldwin documents in “Public Privacy: Restrooms in American Cities, 1869–1932,” temperance advocates made fighting for public bathrooms one of their priorities. After all, once the saloons were shut down, people would still need somewhere to go. Baldwin quotes a 1913 Chicago Tribune article:

Why are we compelled to run the gauntlet past the beer bar, the bartender, and subject to the searching glance of this white-aproned gentleman, until in shame we start to spend money for booze?

Rather than small, minimally private public urinals, temperance activists advocated for large, many-stalled “comfort stations.” But there was a surprising side effect: the privately owned restrooms started to close their gates. (After all, there were public bathrooms available now, so why shouldn’t they only allow in paying customers?)

Meanwhile, as Prohibition played out, the project of constructing public bathrooms slowed to a trickle, and the few that had been built began to fall into disrepair.

The large, underground comfort stations of the early twentieth century are

almost all gone now throughout the United States. City pedestrians are usually forced to rely on facilities in semi-private buildings such as hotels, stores, restaurants, and coffee shops. Instead of a right conferred by government on all citizens, bodily privacy is a purchasable commodity. Even if provided free of charge, the use of the toilet is understood to be the result of an agreement between an individual and a business. It is an awkward, grudging agreement, inflected by judgments of the individual’s social status.

If you’ve ever been wandering the streets of Chicago or New York, wondering why there’s no place to pee, this history is part of the answer.

For the Classroom

  • Men seeking same-sex encounters transformed the pissoir into something its planners never intended. Who ultimately determines the meaning of a public space: its designers, authorities, or the people who use it?
  • The article describes empeche pipi as an early form of hostile architecture. What assumptions about human behavior distinguish architecture designed to prevent an activity from infrastructure designed to accommodate it?
  • What kinds of historical sources would allow us to reconstruct the experiences of people who actually used nineteenth-century public toilets, rather than the intentions of officials who designed and regulated them?
  • Why did temperance advocates in the United States view public restrooms as part of the campaign against alcohol? What does that connection reveal about the unexpected ways infrastructure can influence social behavior?
  • The article ends by describing bodily privacy as a “purchasable commodity” in many American cities. How does the history of public toilets complicate the distinction between public rights and private services?

items.title: Neurodiversity in the Clinic
items.description:
Autism researcher Patrick Dwyer examines how the neurodiversity movement is influencing autism research and clinical decision-making.

The post Neurodiversity in the Clinic appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Some autistic people have long criticized the “medical model” of disability, which treats atypical development as a pathology and seeks to “cure” it, or at least help patients become as close as possible to typically developing peers. An alternative lens popularized in the 1990s by autism rights activist Judy Singer is “neurodiversity.” Autism researcher Patrick Dwyer looks at what this framework could offer professionals working with autistic people and others with differences in neurodevelopment.

Dwyer advocates for a view of neurodiversity that has room for both social factors and individual impairments that may be addressed with treatment, as well as for the idea that neurodivergences can come with strengths. This allows for responses that involve changing the environment and/or helping an individual adapt to their surroundings. For example, responses to ADHD may include offering stimulant medications to help with focus and also removing distractions.

Parents who view their autistic children through a deficit lens may be more likely to pursue ineffective and dangerous pseudoscientific treatments.

Dwyer argues that it’s crucial for neurodivergent people themselves to be the ones deciding which approach to take, to the extent possible. He also distinguishes between interventions to promote well-being and those that aim purely at making people behave more neurotypically, such as trying to suppress harmless autistic “stims” like arm-flapping.

One controversy around the neurodiversity approach involves its application to people with what’s sometimes (controversially) referred to as “severe” or “low-functioning” autism. Parents and caregivers of intellectually disabled or non-speaking autistic people sometimes argue that neurodivergent self-advocates with low support needs can’t speak for those with disabilities that affect their daily lives in more profound ways.

More to Explore

Rethinking Love and Autism

Farah Mohammed
February 14, 2019
Scholars question the common conception that people with Autism Spectrum Disorder don't experience love like neurotypical people do.

But Dwyer suggests that, in practice, the medical model is often simply inapplicable to people with high support needs. For example, there is no pill to help people gain language abilities. Instead, the best-proven interventions are environmental supports like communication tablets and assistance with daily tasks.

Dwyer also argues that a strength-based approach among clinicians, parents, and autistic people themselves can help people with high support needs find the approaches that make most sense for them. Parents who view their autistic children through a deficit lens may be more likely to pursue ineffective and dangerous pseudoscientific treatments.

Meanwhile, for researchers, Dwyer’s neurodiversity approach includes focusing more on environmental factors, which have often been neglected in favor of biological ones, and considering how strengths related to atypical development may help in areas like employment. It also involves looking to autistic self-advocates and conversations within autistic communities for guidance on research directions to pursue. This might include more focus on autistic experiences of sensory overload and meltdowns, as well as the value and pleasure to be found in hyperfocus and intense interest in particular topics.

One stark example here is that, historically, researchers often incorrectly painted autistic people as lacking empathy or even the ability to love. Criticism by autistic individuals led to further research that has found neurotypical researchers may simply fail to see how autistic empathy manifests itself—ironically due to their own lack of empathy for autistic perspectives.

items.title: Ancient Rome: A City of Immigrants
items.description:
A neighborhood beyond the Tiber became home to generations of Jewish and Syrian migrants who reshaped the imperial capital.

The post Ancient Rome: A City of Immigrants appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Big cities bring together peoples from near and far. Magnets for internal migrants and gateways for immigrants, such places tend toward heterogeneity, with spaces for marginalized communities—a pattern that is not just a characteristic of the modern era.

“Ancient Rome was a city of immigrants,” writes historian Ryan R. Abrecht, “a pre-modern metropolis of perhaps a million people at its height, most of them immigrants or the descendants of immigrants.” 

Modern historians overwhelmingly agree that immigration profoundly shaped Rome’s demographics and history, yet some have argued that there was little sense of immigrant community at Rome. In this view, ties between foreigners in the city were weak and mostly ephemeral, even if they shared a common homeland, language or set of religious beliefs.

Abrecht goes on to argue that this was not the case at the neighborhood level, at least in Transtiberim. By the first century CE, the Roman district “beyond the Tiber” had become what we would now call an immigrant neighborhood, a veritable “Little Middle East.”

This district was the heart of Rome’s Jewish and Syrian communities, inhabited for centuries by generations of immigrants from the eastern Mediterranean and their descendants. These residents maintained traditions, languages and customs from home, and participated in civic institutions that helped foster community at the local level.

Founded in the 8th century BCE, Rome was initially confined to the Tiber’s eastern shore. The area west of the river only came under Roman rule in 396 BCE after the defeat of the Etruscans. The west bank was named for its location in relation to the city center. Four centuries later, Augustus incorporated Transtiberim as one of the imperial city’s fourteen administrative districts. In addition to being isolated by the river, Regio XIV was also beyond the pomerium, or religious boundary. This meant unofficial gods—including those of the Jews, Syrians, and later Christians—could be worshipped there. It also meant bodies could be buried there, an important factor for archaeology because of the longevity of funerary inscriptions.

The neighborhood was mocked in satires and condemned for its “panhandlers, prostitutes and desperate people with nowhere else to go.”

Transtiberim was where “noxious or dangerous industries deliberately kept at a distance from central Rome” were located. These included tanning, glassmaking, potting, milling, brick-making and shipping facilities. All these made the neighborhood vibrant and utterly essential to the enormous city.

To elites, who provide almost all the written documentation except for funerary inscriptions, Transtiberim was dangerous, déclassé, and working class (to use later jargon). Strange gods were worshipped there—worship of the Syrian goddess Atargatis by “cross-dressing eunuch priests” who practiced ritual castration was banned more than once. The neighborhood was mocked in satires and condemned for its “panhandlers, prostitutes and desperate people with nowhere else to go.”

More to Explore

Bread, Circuses, Baths: Bathing in Rome, the Public Way

Matthew Wills
December 8, 2025
By the fourth century CE, Rome had some 856 privately owned public baths, the grounds of which served as civic gardens adorned with sculptures.

But the “wrong” side of the river was also home, a community.

Rome’s Jewish community “is one of the oldest in the world, likely originating in the second century BCE.” Unlike in later periods, Transtiberim wasn’t the place Jews were required to live (as in the medieval Venetian ghetto), but as Abrecht notes “there were undoubtedly advantages of living together.” There were also disadvantages: “targeting Jews would also have been especially easy if a large portion of the community was already clustered on the margins of the city.” 

“Many Roman Jews came from Hellenized diaspora communities that used Greek for everyday speech,” writes Abrecht. Syrians were also often fluent in Greek. “Ties of ethnicity, language and religion helped the Jews and Syrians of Transtiberim forge social bonds.”

Abrecht explains that the Latin term Syrus was “ambiguous in ancient literature.” It could mean specifically those from the province of Syria (annexed by Rome in 64 BCE) and/or nearby Phoenicia, Palestine, or Arabia. These could be Semitic peoples or descendants of Greek settlers in that region. With intermarriage common, Syrian identity was “fluid and situational.”

“The immigrants of Transtiberim managed to carve out places for themselves and their children at the heart of the Roman Empire. In doing so, they helped to expand the idea of what it meant to be residents of the imperial city and, more broadly, to be Roman.”

Transtiberim is known as Trastevere today. Perhaps not coincidental to its history, Trastevere has long been Rome’s bohemian neighborhood. The energetic margins may be condemned by the masters of cities, but cities would not be the same without them.
